speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Bissonnette (Minister of State (Small Businesses)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order.
The Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Bissonnette), on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, it seems that the morning papers reported some reference I made to the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), comments which are not on the record as such but which were heard via the sound system of the House of Commons. This morning, I immediately got in touch with the Hon. Member to express my sincere regrets and to apologize.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore wish to make a public apology to the Hon. Member for Hamilton East and formally withdraw the comments attributed to me, although they do not appear in the official record of the proceedings of the House of Commons.

The House resumed from Wednesday, October 30 consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am concerned that we have to join together in this debate on such an important Bill when only this week the all-Party committee, which involved members of the Conservative Party as well as the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, issued what, in a sense, is a rather stunning indictment of the Government's so-called initiatives in the area of employment equity. I refer to suggestions within the report Equality for all-Egalite pour tous-which was received in this House and, I think,
supported very strongly by Members on all sides. The Equality for All Report spoke not only to the need for fundamental legislative changes to incorporate the principles of the Charter of Rights and the Constitution into Canadian law, but also made some very specific recommendations directed at the current legislation before the House, the so-called Employment Equity Bill.
That all-Party committee, which I stress was attended by a majority of Members of the Conservative Party as well as representatives from the Liberal and the New Democratic Parties, pointed out some very serious flaws, flaws which are so serious that even the National Action Committee on the Status of Women-which represents more than three million Canadian women and notwithstanding its long-standing support for promotion of the Employment Equity Program both within the Government and in the private sector, federally and provincially-has been forced to repudiate Bill C-62 because it does not achieve in any small way what it claims to achieve.
Most specifically and ironically, and I think the public should be aware of this, Mr. Speaker, the legislation currently before the House which is being trumpeted by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) as a panacea for the women of Canada, will not apply to the federal Government as an employer. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the federal Government and the Minister of Employment and Immigration introducing a Bill which will not apply to the federal Government as an employer? It will apply only to Crown corporations and to federally regulated corporations with 100 or more employees.
We know that if Bill C-62 is not amended in the way that has been suggested by members of the Liberal Party, the exclusion factor with respect to this Employment Equity Program will mean that 82 per cent of companies under federal regulation will not be touched by the Employment Equity Program. Quite specifically, because the Government and the Minister of Employment have refused to include any provision for businesses with fewer than 100 employees, 3,700 out of 4,500 companies will be excluded; 82 per cent of companies under federal law will not be covered by this legislation. At the same time, the federal Government has excluded itself from the very limpid provisions of Bill C-62.
I believe this Bill irks not only the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, but also a rather rare coalition in Canada which was formed only two weeks ago. We saw major organizations representing women, disabled persons, visible minorities, multicultural minorities and labour getting together to hold a joint press conference to express their dismay at the so-called Employment Equity Bill, which is alleged to be a response to the Abella Report.

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
In my time in Parliament and in the Legislature of Ontario, I have spent a great many hours working toward the notion of equal pay for work of equal value, affirmative action and the over-all employment equity provisions that have been suggested by Judge Abella. However, Judge Abella makes it quite clear that if there is no proper enforcement mechanism, if there are no proper teeth in the law which alleges to give the Canadian Human Rights Commission the right to include plans for employment equity of companies with more than 100 persons, then in fact the law is a fraud, the law is a sham and, in the words of George Bernard Shaw, "the law is an ass". In that particular case I think the Government made serious and believed promises when it entered the women's debate. We remember the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney); he was very strong and very forceful. He said to the Canadian people, in particular to the women of Can "As soon as this Government is elected, the very moment that we are elected, we are going to begin to force companies, which deal with the federal Government, to come into line when it comes to issues of employment equity and affirmative action". Yet, we see that the kind of watered-down version of contract compliance included in Bill C-62 does nothing to ensure the access to equal opportunity promised by the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, we have here a situation where groups such as women, visible and other minorities, the handicapped and labour are getting together and telling the Government: The legislation introduced in the House is a fraud, because the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), that red Tory, is claiming to Canadians that here is a Bill that will help women, minorities and the handicapped. And at the same time, even the largely Conservative Committee that produced the report Equality for All is extensively criticizing the provisions of Bill C-62 now before the House. It is being suggested that certain amendments are needed that will, for instance, give the Human Rights Commission a chance to go to the companies and really make sure that even minor rules that will affect only companies with more than 100 employees, will have enough teeth so something can be done about the situation. Because what is happening now, according to this group of Conservative Members, which includes one Liberal and one New Democrat, is that since the Bill does not apply to the Federal Government, it does not apply to Federal employees, and since it only applies to companies with more than 100 employees, it applies only to about 18 per cent of the companies that are federally regulated.
Mr. Speaker, when women, the handicapped, Conservative Members, the public, labour and people belonging to visible and multicultural minorities all get together to tell the Government: What you are proposing is a fraud, what you are proposing to do is not a genuine response to the promises made by the Prime Minister to women in August 1984: "As soon as I am elected, we are going to start programs that will provide
employment equity for women" .. . Mr. Speaker, what we are seeking, is employment equity for everyone.
The Liberal document produced in the House this week . .. in any case, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-62 provides no answers whatsoever with respect to women's rights, minority rights or rights for the handicapped, and that is why all Canadian men and women are rejecting this legislation, because it is a fraud and an attempt by the Government to live up to promises it never intended to-

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak today on Bill C-62, the employment equity Bill. This is a really inadequate Bill, I am terribly sorry to say. The need for strong action to guarantee genuine equality in the workplace for women, the handicapped, visible minorities and native people has long been recognized. Of course, we have had some very strong recommendations before us, such as those in the Abella Report. We do not see these recommendations being acted on in this legislation.
The NDP caucus has had meetings with representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress, the National Action Committee and other groups that have told us that they are not even remotely satisfied with the action the Government has taken. The National Action Committee on the Status of Women, speaking for millions of Canadian women, has very clearly indicated that the Bill is not adequate and that in principle it is wrong if a Bill is directed toward such a weak array of voluntary measures.
What is wrong with this Bill, Mr. Speaker? The program is voluntary and that is not acceptable at this time. Voluntary programs have been tried before and have been found wanting. They were deemed failures in the United States even though tougher measures were attached. The great wage and salary gaps between women and men are not closing.
The Bill does not provide an enforcement mechanism. This is absolutely crucial and Judge Abella recognized that it was not enough to have a program for affirmative action or employment equity or whatever it is called put in place; there has to be an enforcement mechanism. There is no provision in the Bill for the input of a union where there is an affirmative action or employment equity plan to be developed. Obviously the workers in the workplace would have excellent ideas to contribute. Since they are the ones who are going to be most affected, clearly they ought to have a say in the evolution of these plans.
The Bill does not provide goals and guidelines for affirmative action. It is very vague. It is not directed to anything specific, and not being directed to any specific goals or timetables, we can be jolly sure that nothing will be achieved. A comprehensive affirmative action program would include contract compliance, equal pay for work of equal value, adequate child care measures and a comprehensive education and training plan. This Bill addresses none of these related issues.
October 31, 1985

The whole subject of affirmative action has had a very long history in the United States and that is probably the model to which we have looked. It is not a very positive model for Canadians. In the United States, there were some contract compliance measures and so there were some teeth in the legislation. Companies would actually lose money if they did not come up with affirmative action plans. Here in Canada we have the same model being adopted without the enforcement mechanism, without the teeth and without the threat of lost business. Of course, that threat would be an incentive for a company to introduce a plan.
I suggest that we need to have very careful reporting provisions. There must be concrete guidelines for concrete reports so that we will not have just window dressing types of plans reported. I suggest, for example, that the very simple statistic that ought to be reported by every company doing business with the Government is the proportion of women in the workforce compared with the proportion of the payroll the women receive in the case of comparisons between men and women. Of course, one could do the same for other groups being tested. This statistic would give us a very good indication year after year of whether or not the gap between the two is being reduced. It is only with very firm and objective measures like that that we can ensure there will be real action and not just more window dressing plans allowing the Government to pretend to be doing something about the issue.
I would like to refer to the matter of visible minorities. In my own riding of Broadview-Greenwood, there is a sizeable community of members of visible minorities and many of them tell me about the discrimination they encounter when looking for jobs. They tell me that they are not considered fairly and do not get the same chances. Unfortunately, this has been all too well documented by actual studies. The Urban Alliance on Race Relations has conducted extremely interesting and objective studies. It sent actors and actresses with identical work histories and identical qualifications to potential employers. It was found that those who were members of the white majority were very much better received than members of visible minorities. In one-third of the workplaces tested preference was given to white applicants over non-white applicants who were equally qualified. Will the proposed legislation do anything to remedy this situation? Unfortunately not. Over 50 per cent of employers in this investigation, unsolicited, expressed negative views of racial minorities. Is there any way this legislation will help change that situation? The answer is no.
Some 49 per cent of the complaints by racial minorities of discriminatory behaviour and of racial harassment were dealt with by disciplining the victims, the non-white complainants. Will the proposed legislation in Bill C-62 change that situation? No.
Some 82 per cent of employers have no policy to deal with discrimination in their workplaces and, perhaps, the most disturbing statistic to come out of this study was that 78 per cent of employers do not want policy changes which will
Employment Equity
compel them to eliminate discriminatory practices. Since they are not willing to make these changes voluntarily we must say, as a society, that they do not have that option any more. Equality of our citizens is now written in our law. It is in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is not optional. It is not just a question of people following their own personal tastes in a matter as crucial as the right of other people to earn their livelihoods.
The measures which are before us today are just not remotely up to dealing with these issues. The same can be said for the question of disabled people looking for work. The report Obstacles, which is an excellent federal Government report, deals with the situation of the disabled. The recommendations in that report are much more specific as to what types of measures are needed. Recommendation No. 26 states that a policy should be established of contract compliance for Government contracts with firms employing 100 people or more and involving contracts of more than $20,000. The proposal in Bill C-62 is much less adequate than that. It deals with a much smaller number of firms with larger contracts. Thus the opportunity to bring a large number of businesses under contract compliance legislation has been lost as a result of the wording of the Bill before us.
Recommendation No. 27 of the report Obstacles is that the federal Government should establish an affirmative action compliance board or designate another existing board to develop guidelines and procedures for enforcement, to approve plans and monitor them. It is only with that type of concrete action, with specific plans, with a monitoring mechanism in place and some real penalties that we can ensure that the job will be done. Other countries have done a far better job than Canada has in providing job opportunities for the disabled. The United Kingdom has that type of legislation, as does West Germany and even the United States which is not a pillar in terms of social legislation.
It should be required that managers in the Public Service be accountable for their success in employing and promoting visible minorities, the disabled and women. That aspect should be built into the evaluation plans to ensure that there is action within the Public Service itself. Of course, that is not being done in terms of the Bill which is before us.
I might add that the Province of Saskatchewan, under an NDP Government, brought in such proposals and implemented them. There was beginning to be some movement toward seeing that visible minorities, women and native persons were being given job opportunities. Unfortunately, with the new Conservative Government, those provisions have been watered down. However, we can see that the example went on long enough to know that it was beginning to work, things were beginning to happen and justice was beginning to be done in the workplace.

We are asking for more concerted efforts and mandatory measures, not for the kind of propositions made by this Government in Bill C-62. The Government is advocating weak

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
and non-compulsory measures, but women, visible minorities, native people and disabled persons want-and have earned- equality in the workplace. This Bill falls far short of the mark.
That is why the New Democratic Party will vote against the Bill.

What we want are strong, concrete measures with enforcement, monitoring and evaluation. We really want to encourage the Government to come up with something which will do justice for women who are discriminated against, the handicapped, the disabled and native people. I regret to say that we are voting against Bill C-62 in principle because it does not go far enough. It is not a realistic attack on this problem.

Mr. Speaker, we would not want to vote on this issue without having the opportunity for a thorough debate on Bill C-62. I see the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) in the Chamber and I am sure he would not want that, either. He would want us to discuss this issue fully and throughly in the House of Commons before we vote on this very important measure. We are talking, of course, about employment equity. For many of our constituents this is a relatively new term and perhaps we should identify what employment equity is. Employment equity is the elimination of discrimination and the promotion of employment opportunities among four specific target groups, according to Judge Abella. We are talking about women, native people, disabled persons and the visible minorities. Judge Abella in her report preferred the expression "employment equity" to "affirmative action" or other phrases which have been used in the past. What we all want to do, of course, is to promote and assist those people who need to be equal in relation to all others. In other words, we must put them in a more equitable position with other Canadians because those four target groups have traditionally been greatly disadvantaged.
The purpose of employment equity is to eventually ensure, through this process that we have true equality for all Canadians. We know that we in this country are all equal, at least in theory, according to our Charter of Rights. However, looking at this issue in a more realistic way, we know there is not equity in employment or salaries. For instance, a women earns on average 60 per cent of the salary earned by a man. I hope the day will come very soon when there is real equality in this country but, unfortunately, notwithstanding all of the good intentions which collectively we all have, we are not approaching that stage nearly soon enough.
I would like to refer to some of the background of this issue of employment equity. I referred a few moments ago to the report of Judge Rosalie Abella which was commissioned in June of 1983 by the then Minister of Employment and Immigration. A report was tabled in this House in November of 1984. I am sure you recall that day very vividly, Mr. Speaker. Judge Abella's recommendations to this House were, in brief, that we should bring forward legislation enacting mandatory
employment equity for employers under federal jurisdiction- all of them. She recommended that we should be persuading provincial Governments to adopt similar legislation in the areas of provincial jurisdiction, and the recommended contractual compliance for all federally-regulated employers. Finally, she recommended that we establish an agency to enforce mandatory employment equity, and four options were enumerated. But what have we done?
Let us review the Bill that we are talking about today. I want to remind Hon. Members across the way that the Bill has no mandatory enforcement of employment equity at all. There are no provisions for a separate monitoring agency. The responsibility has been conferred upon the Canadian Human Rights Commission. The Canadian Human Rights Commission will have no power to enforce employment equity. There have been no targets set by the Government or the Minister, no standardization in reporting procedures, and no penalties for companies that do not comply. The Minister said that that is all right because public opinion will ultimately be the judge of those who do wrong. I ask Members across the way, since when do we as Canadians offer justice to our minorities based on a popularity contest? That is what the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is asking us to do through this Bill.

In other words, the Minister seems to think that we will have to wait for the findings of a public opinion poll before the situation can be set straight-nothing will change unless the people voice their opposition, and then justice will flow from this measure. I have to ask the Hon. Member opposite whether he really believes a popularity constest is the best way to solve the problem.
Well, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding what he might say now, I think he is a fair man and I wonder whether he would agree that the Bill should provide mechanisms to ensure full compliance with the new legislation on the part of Government agencies and the various companies which are awarded Government contracts. Mr. Speaker, it is not good enough to say that Canadians need only be informed and that it will be up to them to judge whether an agency or company has failed to follow the ministerial directives.

During the last election campaign the Conservatives promised many things to many people.
Hear, hear!

Someone says "hear, hear". I was not intending to go into great detail, but I will remind that Member that there is a little book containing 338 Tory promises which I have talked about in the House on one or two occasions. Anyone who wants a copy of the book need only contact my office and I will gladly send one. That offer includes Members across the way and Canadians across Canada as well.
October 31, 1985

I will outline some of the promises that the Tories made to Canadian women. The Conservatives said that they would institute major training and retaining programs to ensure that women are prepared for the new occupations of the technological era. What happened to that promise? They also said that they would make clear to companies doing business with the federal Government that their performance in hiring and promoting women will be a key factor in obtaining contracts for goods and services. What happened to that promise? Why is Bill C-62 based on public opinion, instead of making it clear as was promised in that commitment? Could it be that the Conservatives have broken a promise? Maybe it was a sacred trust, in which case we can be sure that it has been broken because all the sacred trusts were broken a long time ago.
Another sacred trust of the Tories was that they would make the federal public service a model to be followed with regard to the equality of women in the workplace. What happened to that promise? Why does this promise not coincide with what is included in Bill C-62? Mr. Speaker, as much as I have to say it, I think the Tories broke another promise. It does not surprise some of us that some promises have been broken. Why does the Minister not stand up in the House and tell us that she will improve this Bill and make it coincide with what the Conservative Party promised the women of Canada and others during the election campaign of last year? I urge her to do that now.

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) said, Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, is a Bill about opportunity. It demands that employers take special measures to ensure that our aboriginal people, our disabled, our women and our visible minorities will not be denied work opportunities because of their sex, colour or handicap. This debate reminds me of the time when a six-year old black girl on a very dirty, dusty road in her village in Tanzania adopted me as her white man. She had no fear, prejudice or discrimination. The Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) spoke on this Bill with regard to some of the acts of discrimination which he has experienced. I, for one, do not doubt him for a moment since he is black. I can relate closely to what he said because of my own African experiences. The incident with that little black girl, whose name I do not even know, has impressed me to this day so much that I now feel totally colour blind. I am proud to say that as a member of this truly great national Government I am making history, along with my colleagues, in ensuring that all our people-and I emphasize the word "all" -will now be treated equally with retard to opportunities in the workplace.
Equality is of paramount importance and concern to Canadians, especially new Canadians. The provisions of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which were entrenched in April of this year, state:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age, or mental or physical disability.
Employment Equity
The royal commission report on equality in employment, more often referred to in this House as the Abella Report, noted that the hope of the four designated groups was that "as quickly as possible, they would be transformed from being objects in the political laboratory to being subjects of political action". Mr. Speaker, Bill C-62 shows a willingness on the part of the Government to do just that, and it has been done in record time. The Abella Report continues, on page 23, to say the following:
Yet for all their differences, the one issue about which there was general agreement among the groups was the need for strong government measures to ensure equality in employment.
This is exactly what we are doing with the targeted areas of federal responsibility. How many times have you heard an employer say that he would not hire a black, a Paki, a women or a disabled person? I think we have heard that all too often, Mr. Speaker. To me this attitude is mindless and it demonstates a degree of bigotry that is all too prevalent in Canada. Bill C-62 does not go all the way, but it is a pretty positive start to changing, not only the law, but the attitude of many Canadian employers.
There is a company in my riding called BDM Co Operative Warehouse Service of Canada Ltd. which does business with the Government and wants to do more. It is presently negotiating to buy or lease a vacant Government building in Ottawa-Carleton on Walkley Road. In so doing it will kill a number of birds with one stone. It intends to use the building to provide first class private sector services to the Government for storage facilities of files and documents. The beauty of the project, Mr. Speaker, is that the company intends to hire 40 or 50 disabled persons to do the work. That is very good news and that is why I am doing all I can to assist that company. That is an obvious immediate response to Bill C-62. That the arms and legs of handicapped persons do not function the same as those of more normal persons does not mean that their minds are poor. They cannot always work at the same speed as others, but they probably make fewer mistakes. There are many jobs that these people can do if given a fair chance. Some Members opposite have called for more affirmative action. There are Government programs in existence now that are tougher than Bill C-62 because departments must submit plans to Treasury Board for approval in advance with respect to hiring the four designated groups. Let me say, for the sake of the cynics, that we are not throwing the merit principle out of the window in the Public Service or federally regulated businesses. However, systemic discrimination and other forms of discrimination must be eradicated in all areas of federal jurisdiction as soon as possible.
I was proud to assist a young woman in her late twenties to find employment with Labour Canada recently. Her name is Janet. She suffers from cerebral palsy as a result of difficulties at birth. Today, she walks with the aid of two crutches.
Through the excellent co-operation of Diane Dufresne, who is a director in the National Capital Region's staffing office of the Public Service, and Suzanne Azzie, who is co-ordinator of

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
employment services for disabled persons, Janet is now working very well and is very happy as a full time clerk in the Public Service. In fact, for the first time in her life, she is living in her own apartment in Ottawa.
I liken this to one small step for Janet which will be translated into miles for many other deserving capable Canadians.
There has been much talk by the Opposition about the lack of enforcement mechanisms and penalties for companies that do not abide by Bill C-62. Let me assure you that we will not set up another bureaucracy to monitor results. We know that we have enough of that at the municipal, provincial, national and international levels. We do not want, nor do we need more bureaucracy.
With respect to enforcement, the Government is modelling its enforcement plans after what is called Model Four in the Abella Report. Guidelines are now being prepared by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission, known as CEIC, and will be shared with employers along with free consultative assistants. Collection of data will be done by CEIC. Data will be made available to the Human Rights Commission as well as to individuals and groups.
Investigation and adjudication of disputes under Section 32.3 of the Canadian Human Rights Act empowers the commission to initiate complaints where reasonable grounds exist. The data will provide such grounds. The Human Rights Commission will be strengthened, if necessary, to enable it to carry out this role. Contract compliance is being introduced, along with enforcement mechanisms. CEIC will monitor contractors and advise the contracting Minister of companies who do not live up to their commitments. These companies may be barred from future contracts.
With respect to Labour Canada inspectors, the Government will ensure that the Canadian Human Rights Commission has the staff necessary to monitor their settlements. The Labour Canada inspectors now have the authority to refer complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission in the case of equal pay, and they have a specific mandate to do so under Section 38.1 of the Labour Code. It is thus clear that the Government's mechanisms for enforcement are consistent with those recommended by Judge Abella in Option Four. The specific organizations involved reflect the Government's desire to utilize existing mechanisms rather than create new ones.
Judge Abella has said that achievements will be measured by results, not quotas, as some have suggested. The affected companies will set their own goals to meet their particular situation, such as the case of BDM in my riding to which I referred.
The question of sanctions have been of some concern. I would like to address that question as well. Bill C-62, as recommended by Judge Abella, requires employers throughout the federal sector with 100 employees or more to implement employment equity programs. The Bill will also require them to demonstrate the results of their implementation by annually reporting their results.
The measures outlined in the Bill respond to Recommendation Nos. 3, 6 and 7 of the Abella Commission. Let me paraphrase those recommendations. They recommend that no quotas should be imposed, employers should be given flexibility in the redesign of their employment practices, and results, not systems, should be reviewed initially.
Employers now know that they need to identify and eliminate practices which discriminate against target group members. If one refers to Clause 5 and Clause 6 of the Bill, one can see quite clearly that clause 5 states that employers must file reports. In terms of sactions, Clause 6 reads:
An employer who fails to comply with section 5 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand dollars.
Let us not forget that lobby groups will keep the pressure on business and Government and that this is to be encouraged. The potential for lawsuits on the entrenched rights in the Constitution maintain the pressure.
More important, Bill C-62 concerns fairness. Employment equity is a concept based on the belief of fairness and opportunity. Those realizing the economic benefits of employment should comprise all aspects of the Canadian population. The Bill aims to achieve results with the co-operation of employers in the federally regulated business sector. My Government and I believe that that approach can and will be effective.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, you ask whether the House is ready for the question. I am certainly not ready for the question. A number of Members on this side of the House want to make a contribution to the debate on this legislation. I want to assure you that the House will not be ready for the question for some time.
The Bill before the House today concerns employment equity, or affirmative action. Let me commence by briefly explaining the importance of affirmative action and why we are urging the Government to implement a positive and effective affirmative action program. Affirmative action is fundamental to our values in a society which firmly believes in equality of opportunity and condition. Since we value the opportunity for people to participate in society as a whole, our citizens must have the fullest opportunity to develop as individuals and the community must have access to the full potential of its human resources. We do not want to see anyone in our society excluded from that participation. It is only on the basis of each person being given an opportunity to develop and become productive in society that we can have a community in which we can have pride and a sense of security.
Affirmative action is a means of confirming our value of equality in Canadian life. It has long been stated that Canadian society is far from equal and that a number of groups in Canadian society are far from reaching that goal of equality.
I want to refer to the status of women in our society. One glaring example of inequality is the fact that for each dollar earned by men, women earn only 60 cents. While women have
October 31, 1985

made significant advances in employment in the last couple of decades, the remuneration they receive is inadequate and far less than what a man would receive in similar circumstances. We must address this problem through affirmative action. Furthermore, it follows that women's pensions will be 60 per cent of the pension of their male counterparts. The vast majority of Canadians are not willing to tolerate this kind of inequality.
We have in our society a number of visible minorities, including black and Asian people.
The inequality of visible minorities in Canada is a worry which I am sure many Canadians have when they look south across the border and see what has happened with the black people, particularly in the cities. Not only to see the potential of individuals fulfilled, but also to see that our communities are ones in which we can live in peace, comfort and enjoyment, it is important that visible minorities be given full opportunity, particularly in the area of employment.
The same inequality exists for the handicapped. The handicapped are in many ways excluded from our society by architecture because few buildings are accessible to the handicapped, a situation that needs to be changed. Buildings are only a symbol of the way we bar access to equal opportunity for handicapped individuals. Other changes are needed, changes in employment policies and in recruitment procedures. What about opportunities for training? The vast majority of Canadians would like the Government to take effective action to ensure that handicapped people have equal access to opportunity and employment and to see that society benefits from the rich resources of the handicapped.
Another group of people who stand out in terms of inequality and call upon us to establish effective affirmative action programs are the native people. If we look at native people in the poor areas of cities, such as Winnipeg and other western cities, we find that poverty is intolerable. It is visible. People live in inadequate housing and have a low level of education. Unemployment is in the area of 60 per cent. These are not official statistics but educated guesses. If we look at native people in rural areas on reserves, we find that unemployment is in the area of 80 per cent to 90 per cent. Greater equality is needed.
The need for affirmative action is based upon lack of equality. Most Canadians want a society in which people have equality of opportunity and human condition.
This Bill before the House falls far short of what could be called effective affirmative action. The Bill is a voluntary program rather than a mandatory one. We know from the United States experience and from our own experience here with regard to voluntary programs that we need a mandatory program with deadlines, goals and specific objectives.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):
Employment Equity
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-62, an Act respecting Employment Equity be not now read a second
time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.
I move this motion, Mr. Speaker, because the Government needs more time to find out about why this Bill falls far short of an adequate affirmative action program. The Government needs to rethink its position. We need the six months for the Government to come up with an effective affirmative action program.
