speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment introduced by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper). I think the purpose of his amendment, which is to give some time for the Government to come to its senses, is a very important one. Not that I have much confidence that that will happen because we have seen over the past 18 months that you cannot come to your senses if you do not have much sense to begin with. At the same time, being a Liberal I am an eternal optimist and live in hope that at some point in time Members opposite will understand fully what a serious betrayal they are perpetrating on the Canadian people by this Bill.
In the spring of 1983, I was engaged in what I thought was one of the more important initiatives as a Minister of the Crown. I received from my Cabinet the approval to establish the Abella Commission. It was important because at that time I saw it as a major turning point in the evolution that had been under way for the past two decades, which was to bring about a higher and greater sense of understanding and consciousness about the need for equality rights.
The Abella Commission was established for an important reason. In a simple way, the voluntary system to achieve affirmative action that had been put in place up to that time had failed. Every single Conservative speaker who has risen to speak in this House has said, "Let us give the voluntary system a chance", which shows that Conservatives are incapable of understanding history or they are blind to what went on before. There was a voluntary system, Mr. Speaker.
The Department of Employment and Immigration had a special division to provide assistance to private employers and municipalities to engage in the development of voluntary affirmative action programs. Four years of effort to achieve that
8198

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
resulted in something like 100 companies of the 50,000 or
60,000	companies in Canada showing any interest in signing up or developing an affirmative action program. They all had the resources they needed and all the support. All the things that are supposedly going to happep as a result of this Bill have happened before. This Bill simply puts up a masquerade instead of a program that has already ostensibly failed. That is why it is such a betrayal.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) knows full well that that method will not work. She was the critic from 1982 to 1983. She stood on her feet time and time again and said, with no sense of uncertainty, that we needed mandatory contract compliance to make it work. Now that she is the Minister, she totally denies a position which she held for many years. That is an act of betrayal by that Minister of a constituency which, as she said, she represented for many years. It is a betrayal of a clear understanding of the facts, and now it is a betrayal of what was to be an important achievement in terms of legislating the requirements at the federal level for private companies and Crown corporations to introduce a proper system of affirmative action.
I have gone over the Debates of the House carefully. It is an ironic tragedy that the Conservative Members of Parliament who have spoken on the Bill have been so blind and untrustworthy when it comes to the actual achievement of affirmative action. The Government is engaged in one of the most serious breaches of trust.
We can all remember the flourishing words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) during debate in the summer of 1984 when he was asked about the Abella Commission and what he would do. He held his hand to his heart and with that incredible sense of insincerity, which we have now come to know, love and admire, said that he was fully committed to contract compliance. What a difference a year makes! What a difference an election makes! What has happened to those firm and unalterable words of the Prime Minister? I guess the same thing happened to them as has happened to almost every other commitment he has made.
The record and history of mandatory programs of affirmative action show that they work. Along with the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), I, as Minister responsible, introduced into the Public Service the requirement for affirmative action in Departments. It was begun on a trial basis in 1981 with three Departments. The system and methodology were tested. We introduced it in 1980-81 to the Treasury Board, the Secretary of State Department and the Department of Employment and Immigration. We put in place a method to demonstrate clearly how such a system could work and be effective. Then, in 1983, the program was introduced to cover all government Departments.
The next step in the blueprint was to extend it to Crown corporations and all industries which were then under federal jurisdiction. The Abella Commission was established to determine the most effective formula for that third step. It was not
a commission of study. It was not established to ascertain the facts. We all knew that there was a continuing and unacceptable inequality when it came to the employment rights of women, the handicapped, native people and visible minorities. The Abella Commission did not have to ascertain those facts; they were known. The task of Judge Abella was to determine the most effective formula, based upon intensive consultation with private business, Crown corporation leaders and provincial Governments.
The report was tabled, and that formula was clearly accepted and applauded across the country. It was accepted because Judge Abella put her finger on one fundamental ingredient in any affirmative action program, that is, that we could not rely upon individual companies, corporations and organizations to introduce a program for their own organizations when they did not know whether their competitor across the street, or other organizations with which they did business, would do the same. Therefore they said: "Why would I accept an unfair advantage? Why would I go to the extra cost of introducing affirmative action when no one else is going to do it?" It does involve extra cost to introduce affirmative action. The basic, fundamental flaw in a voluntary program is that unless it is universal and unless the same rules apply to everyone, individual companies or organizations will not do it. Even those well-intentioned presidents of corporations who saw the necessity and the imperative need for affirmative action told me when I was Minister of Employment that they would like to do it, but that they would not do so because their competitors would not do it and therefore they would be unable to compete with them on an equal level. They said: "If we are going to do it, we all have to do it". That is also what Judge Abella said and, therefore, that it was essential to have a mandatory requirement. As well, she pointed out the importance of introducing the contract compliance ingredient.
It was clear that the provinces, particularly the Conservative Governments of those provinces, would not do it. A meeting of provincial Minister was convened in 1982 by the then Secretary of State to talk about the introduction of equality rights, and it was the provincial Governments which opposed it at that time. Judge Abella carefully said that if we were to provide for a further clear step forward, it must be done at the federal level.
The report was tabled. The recommendations were made. The Minister of Employment and Immigration rose in the House and declared with the greatest of flourish and fervor how wonderful the report was. What happened thereafter? Then the Government came out with Bill C-62, which is not even a pale imitation. It is a betrayal. It is a denial. It is a treasonous act against all those who have worked for years to try to bring about substantial improvement in the lives of many Canadian workers. There is nothing in Bill C-62 in which Parliament can take pride. Therefore, it makes eminent sense for us to support the amendment. Those Conservative Members who in their heart of hearts know that it is a Bill which is simply a paper masquerade, should try to put some pressure upon Cabinet, which has made the wrong choice, a
October 31, 1985

serious mistake and has betrayed women, the handicapped, native people and visible minorities. That is what the Bill is all about. It will go down in the long history of trying to achieve equality rights as one of the blackest moments.
Oh, oh!
And the only response we get from the Tories is that they laugh about it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-62 and on the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper).
This employment equity Bill is really a missed opportunity. Because that is so, we in the New Democratic Party have great difficulty supporting it. There are several reasons for that difficulty. The Bill really calls for a voluntary program, which is clearly unacceptable to my Party.
Voluntary affirmative action programs have been tried in several jurisdictions other than in Canada-most notably, in the United States, Germany and other European countries- and it was found that they simply did not work. In the United States, in particular, it was decided in the 1960s to come forward with mandatory programs, which have proven to be quite effective.
I, along with other Members from all sides of the House, had the opportunity in 1980, after the election campaign, to form an all-Party committee of the House of Commons to look into problems affecting the disabled population. We came up with a number of recommendations which, if implemented, could have been of great assistance to disabled Canadians in their attempt to participate in the mainstream of Canadian society.
I would like to centre my remarks on the disabled community rather than on women, natives or other groups as other members of my caucus have already addressed themselves to those groups. The committee recognized that most of the problems affecting the disabled community centred on the key issue of employment opportunity. One can talk about the social needs of that particular group in any terms one wishes, whether it be in terms of access to housing, access to transportation, education, recreation, information or even technical aids. These things cannot be separated one from the other. Each one is connected to the other. One cannot talk about providing an individual with access to education on all levels including post-secondary education without also talking about how that individual can be productively employed following the receipt of his or her education, and this is assuming that the individual can get into the educational system to begin with.
As the committee went across the country speaking to Canadians, it heard numerous stories indicating that there are literally thousands of children who are denied access to education because of their disabilities. This Bill does not address
Employment Equity
that problem. It does not address training opportunities for people who happened to be disabled. Unless we talk about that in a very real and concrete way, we cannot talk about employment opportunities because one is synonymous with the other.
We cannot talk about employment opportunities without talking about how we allow the individual to be moved from the place of residence to the place of employment. It must be recognized that most modes of transportation are not designed to be used by physically disabled people. We have to talk about these things in a very real and basic way. This Bill does not do that. It does not even touch upon that.
I find it surprising that the Government would introduce a measure like this. I can only conclude that the reason it did so was that it recognized there is a public sentiment in favour of providing equity to the various diverse groups in our society, but the Government did not want to go too far because of the pressures from other areas of society, primarily employers. I have been told that that is indeed the case. The Government has caved in to the pressure from that elite group of society against the best interests of those who really need society's help in order to move within the mainstream of society. I think that that is rather shameful. If I view this Bill as being purely a public relations effort rather than a real effort to help people, I am going to have great difficulty in supporting it, even though it goes a bit further than anything introduced by the previous Government.
I listened with some interest to the Member who just spoke, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). In his previous capacity as a Minister, he appeared before the committee to give testimony. I must say that he was generally sympathetic toward affirmative action programs. However, he could afford to be generally sympathetic because the rest of his Cabinet opposed them.
Come, come!

The Hon. Member scoffs. It is on the record. It is contained in the transcripts of the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. It is recorded there for posterity and it cannot be disputed.
I am glad to hear that there are other members of that previous Government who now support mandatory affirmative action programs. They certainly did not do so before. If they had done so before, perhaps that influence would have been felt by the present Gouvernment, which indeed needs some education in this field. That is why I am pleased that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, moved the amendment. If we give the Government another six months to give more thought to this Bill, I am sure it will do the right thing. The right thing is to bring in affirmative action programs that mean something.
There is a concern felt by the Government that if we were to bring in an affirmative action program, it would be disruptive to industry. That has not been the case where affirmative action programs exist. I will speak of those in the United States because it is of close relationship to our jurisdiction. When the special committee had the opportunity of speaking

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
to public figures and indeed members of the corporate sector in the United States, it found that they did not have any problems with affirmative action programs in so far as they concerned the disabled community. In fact, they found that as those programs worked, they allowed members of the disabled community to support themselves within society and to be productive members of society. In fact, they boasted to us on several occasions that a disabled individual was equal to or even a better productive worker than an able-bodied individual. That has been the experience in the United States. The Government of Canada should not have any great concern that affirmative action would be disruptive in some way. In fact, it would have a very beneficial and positive result.
An initiative on which the previous Government refused to act because of pressure from industry, and not even Canadian industry which supported the initiative, was to make telephones fully compatible with hearing aids. It requires only a small coil to be placed in a telephone to make it totally compatible with hearing aids. Bell Canada and other Canadian telephone manufacturers support that initiative. The problem is with imported telephones that are not compatible with hearing aids. This threatens the job security of people who are hard of hearing. If the Government wanted to do something before six months was up, it could move in that direction and order that all telephones coming into the country be compatible with hearing aids.
I see that you are signalling that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. That is very unfortunate. There is a great deal more that I would like to say on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a contribution to this debate on employment equity. I am in a good position to do so because the riding I represent, Saint-Leonard-Anjou, is home to many community groups who live and work there. Practically every Saturday morning many people and members of those cultural communities drop in my riding office to express their deep concern about their chances of getting good jobs and the possibility of their children ever being able to work in the Public Service of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-62 does not give any assurance to those people, and that is why I rise in the House this morning to urge my colleagues on the Government benches to work with us so that we might indeed assure the various communities of a fair share in Canadian society, a fair share of Canadian jobs.
I was rather disappointed yesterday when I saw the Minister of State (Multiculturalism) (Mr. Jelinek) rise in the House and, instead of telling us more about those programs and what he is prepared to do for cultural communities in Canada, criticize my colleague from York West (Mr. Marchi) for allegedly wasting time to send out press releases instead of asking more questions in the House. It is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker! Instead of telling us how he will convince his Cabinet colleagues to restore the confidence of our cultural communities by assuring them that they are equal partners and full-fledged members of Canadian society, our Minister responsible for those cultural communities stands up in the House to criticize and make fun of Members who are doing their job.
I have something else to say about this, Mr. Speaker. One of the Progressive Conservative Party's election campaign was to look after cultural communities but, at the first opportunity, the multiculturalism portfolio was given to a Minister with joint responsibilities. We have a Minister responsible for amateur sport and multiculturalism. That is how much importance this Government attaches to Canada's cultural communities!
Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to another very important question which is not even mentioned in Bill C-62, yet it has been the subject of equality rights committee recommendations. I am talking about the question of the wife or spouse with respect to Revenue Canada. I am a strong supporter of institutional marriage, but still one must keep an open mind and face reality. A great many people live together in what is usually known as common law marriages. Mr. Speaker, those people cannot avail themselves of the various tax benefits which allow deductions, asset transfers and other arrangements. I should think that Canadian society is mature enough to take a close look at the situation and make it possible for those fellow citizens-regardless of their condition or marital status-to enjoy the same benefits as you and I and other Canadians take for granted.
Another point I want to make this morning relates to the case of disabled persons, for it is our responsibility to make sure they do have a place in our society. And this is why, Mr. Speaker, we must make sure that we have employment policies, that we help them get jobs and that we provide the means of transportation they need to go to work. Of course, our tax system fails to satisfy either the individual himself or the employer who is willing to hire the handicapped.
Mr. Speaker, as legislators, we must give a clear signal to all Canadians, to our employers, to our public servants and to our administrative officers that they must change their attitude in order to enable the handicapped, the people of various ethnic communities and the visible minorities to have access to all our programs and services as well as to our job opportunities.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure my constituents of Saint-Leonard-Anjou that as their representative in this House, I will do my utmost to defend their rights so that they may always feel that they are full-fledged citizens of this great country we call Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we oppose Bill C-62 and we support the hoist motion for what I think are well documented and well established reasons. We do
October 31, 1985

not feel that the Bill takes the right type of action toward ensuring that we will have affirmative action.
By putting the hoist motion before the House we are giving the Government an opportunity to reassess the contents of its Bill. If it does not do that, then Bill C-62 can be dubbed the Bill of lost opportunity What the Government has here is an opportunity to do something about job equity in the country. We know from experience, not only in Canada but from all over the world, that it is quite a simple matter to pay lip service to changes in the type of structures which our country has developed.
After the Civil War in the United States the slaves were emancipated. However, it took another 100 years before there was any effect on changing discrimination against blacks. That only took place when legislation was put in place and the courts made decisions forcing people to adhere to the legislation. That is what the Government has the opportunity to do with respect to this particular Bill.
All of the Parties in the House gave major support to the Abella Report. However, Bill C-62 backs off from that report. In fact, one would think that the people who drafted the Bill forgot entirely about the Abella Report. In fact, one can easily recognize that the attempts here are simply a matter of paying lip service, a cosmetic move, to have something appear to be done. They also forgot about all the other reports of commissions which have been laid before the House and other public statements which have been made by a variety of public-oriented groups and organizations.
We are opposing the Bill and supporting the hoist motion for what we consider to be good and acceptable reasons. The first reason is that it is a voluntary program and we know that voluntary programs have not worked in the past. The Bill does not provide any type of enforcement mechanism. Surprisingly, it has an enforcement mechanism with respect to the gathering of data to ensure that corporation report. However, it does not put into place any type of penalty or any enforcement mechanism with regard to the actual affirmative action which it pretends to be putting into the employment structure of the country. If affirmative action is going to be developed, or is developed in a particular corporation, there is no suggestion in this Bill that the employees, the workers or the union should have a part in putting in place the kind of affirmative action which would work better. We have learned over the years that if we really want something to work, it must have the support of the employees as well as of management.
This Bill does not even give specific goals or objectives for companies which do start in this direction. It does not establish a level which they should be expected to achieve at any particular time. What is necessary is a program which would require contract compliance, equal pay for work of equal value, adequate job care measures and a comprehensive education and training plan. This legislation has none of these provisions.
Employment Equity
Many organizations have made this point to the Government. It is not as if the Government passed a Bill and then later found out that many organizations did not support it, all of the organizations which are involved have told the Government that the Bill is inadequate. It is not a matter of the Government not knowing. Since it has not taken action, the six-month hoist might possibly give it the opportunity to do so.
The United States, because it is close to us, is a good example of what does not happen if there is voluntary affirmative action. It was tried in the United States for years and it did not work. So why should we expect this Bill to work?
Women, the disabled and visible minorities have all indicated that they do not think this Bill will work. I suggest that this Bill flies in the face of the Abella Report which indicated that the voluntary element of this program with mandatory reporting requirements is nonetheless voluntary, therefore, it does not require a remedy to be put in place. It does not require a remedy to the discriminatory practice disclosed when the information comes in. When the reports come in from the corporations indicating that they have done something but have not done enough to satisfy the situation, there is no requirement that they produce a program which would have some impact on employment equity.
I have a number of letters, press releases and so on from a variety of groups. The National Action Committee on the Status of Women opposes the passage of Bill C-62 without previsions which guarantee mandatory affirmative action programs with targets. The Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women is concerned that Bill C-62 will not achieve its stated purpose to achieve equality in the workplace. The Coalition of Visible Minorities stated:
Clearly, the proposed legislation is not an effective vehicle for dismantling structural inequities.
Without an enforcement mechanism, without sanctions, there is simply no reason to expect that employment equity can be achieved.
I could refer to any one of those groups and spend 10 minutes in speaking about how they feel that Bill C-62 does not fulfil these requirements. Since I do not have the time to do so, I will conclude by saying that the Government has now before it a six-month hoist possibility. That could be a time in which the Government could make sure that the Bill does what it says it should do.

Mr. Speaker, Clause 2 of Bill C-62, which is before us today, has as its purpose, and 1 quote:
-to achieve equality in the work place so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfillment of that goal, to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the same way but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences.
That is a very laudable purpose, but when one looks through the Bill for ways in which this purpose is to be achieved, one finds that the only requirement is for reporting. Certain employers are required to report on their staffing patterns.

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
They are required to report on the industrial sector in which the employees are employed, the location, and the number of persons and designated groups so employed. There is a fine for not filing the report annually. So there is a fine for failing to report but there is no sanction whatsoever for failing to do. Nor is there any assistance offered or any clear guidelines. We read that the Minister "may" make guidelines.
I would assume that the reason we only have a reporting provision is that the Government is relying on the reporting and on the publication to create, perhaps, a certain climate of public opinion and certain public pressure on employers to come into line.
Ten years ago, I would have supported this kind of notion of voluntary sanctions or, at least, voluntary encouragement. Most Canadians generally, I think, respond to encouragement and persuasion rather than to coercion. However, we tried for over 10 years. We have had various systems of voluntary compliance and there has been very little progress. I am sure that most employers do not set out to discriminate against women, the handicapped, Canadian Indians and visible minorities, but it is often just more comfortable and simpler to hire the kind of person you know. It is often thoughtlessness rather than deliberate discrimination.
Financial factors enter into the case of the handicapped. To accommodate wheelchairs one must have wider doors, ramps instead of stairs and wider elevators. What one hears from employers-indeed, as my colleague from Winnipeg said earlier-is: "Why should I add to my cost of doing business if my competitors are not required to do so?" That is also an argument for mandatory requirements which apply equally to everyone.

I was in the House, Mr. Speaker, as you were, when the human rights code was amended to include the concept of equal pay for work of equal value. I believe that may have been the case in 1975. At that time we hoped that the amendments would lead to a considerable improvement in the economic status of women in the public service and of other disadvantaged groups. At that time we thought that giving the right of complaint and setting up procedures within the Human Rights Commission was an adequate way of redressing those grievances. It has not proved to be so, Mr. Speaker. It is now time to recognize that the complaints method has not worked. That method puts the onus on the employee to make the employer observe the law. It is now time to recognize that that puts an unfair load on the employee. It has not worked because the system is cumbersome. Many employees find it difficult and it is now time to make employers obey the law.
The commission headed by Judge Rosalie Abella, which examined the problems of employment equity, came up with some far-reaching recommendations. The Government has chosen not to adopt them, but to bring in a Bill which relies only on reporting. In terms of contract compliance, we are told that the employment equity requirements will apply only to contracts over $200,000. This includes only about 100 of the
25,000	to 30,000 companies with which the Government deals and it effectively excludes small business, the largest creator of jobs in Canada. The thinking may have been that if the 100 largest companies were required to set an example, other companies would follow them. Since voluntary measures of one kind and another relying on public opinion have not been effective until now, surely it is time to move on to new methods.
The only redress for an employee under Bill C-62 continues to be the Human Rights Commission, which is expected to monitor these reports without any formal extension of its mandate and without any increase in funding. We know that the Human Rights Commission has an enormous backlog at the moment. The Auditor General's Report which was tabled yesterday referred to it. It is simply not feasible to think that the Human Rights Commission will be able to do this additional work under those circumstances.
Let us look at some of the groups representing people covered by this Bill which have criticized the Bill as not going far enough. The National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, the National Ethnocultural Council, the Canadian Association for Community Living, formerly the Canadian Association for the Mentally Retarded, the Urban Alliance for Race Relations, and the Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women are unanimous in saying that the Government's response to the Abella report, as represented in this Bill, is weak, ineffective, and a betrayal of the commitments and promises made to them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret that the Hon. Member's time has expired. I will recognize the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to speak on this Bill and specifically on the amendment just introduced by the New Democratic Party to delay the implementation of the Bill until it can be changed. I want to take this opportunity to read into the record some suggestions for change from a group called S.U.C.C.E.S.S.
Are they Tories?

The Hon. Member asks whether they are Conservatives. I think this is a non-partisan group. It is the United Chinese Community Enrichment Services Society. It was formed in 1973 to help members of the Vancouver and Lower Mainland Chinese community overcome language and cultural barriers, to assume greater responsibility toward selfreliance, and to contribute fully to Canadian society. Last year the group served 42,250 people, which is quite a record. They are interested in the creation of employment equity for disadvantaged groups in our society.
I have a copy of a letter written to the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) by Sandra Wilking, who is the chairperson of the board of directors. She makes five suggestions which I would like to put on the record in order that they can be considered by the Government in
October 31, 1985

changing the Bill. First, she says that the possibility of expanding the definition of "designated groups" should be looked at to include minorities, for example, people from Mediterranean and Latin American backgrounds. These peole are just as disadvantaged as visible minority groups because, like the visible minority groups, they have limited knowledge of the English language with which to function in the workplace.
Second, she says that the Government should look at the possibility of including in the employer group unions that fall under federal jurisdiction. This group is also a potential group of employers.
Third, she says that they are concerned that the current proposed legislation remains silent on the enforcement factor. Who will be responsible for ensuring that there are positive results toward employment equity in the employer groups? Who will police the Act? The fine of $5,000 is not as effective as specific performance and other remedies, according to S.U.C.C.E.S.S.
The fourth point they make is that the current Bill is not clear on what types of relevant data would be required in the employers' reports. There may be data, for example on the number of applications from the designated group for a particular job opening and a number of appointments made in ratio with the number of application, and that data should be forthcoming.
Fifth, if an employer is to recruit for the various target groups, as outlined in the Act, it would seem that the relevant questions should be asked on the application form. This would include the ethnicity question and the group suggests that Anglo Saxon should be included as an ethnic background.
These are a number of interesting suggestions and I offer them to the Government. I certainly agree with one point in particular, that is, that there is no enforcement mechanism in this Bill. It is not good enough, Mr. Speaker, just to rely on reporting. We need some teeth. The subject is too important to ignore.
I would like to say something generally about employment equity. I would like to express some of my own views in this particular area. Employment equity is a polite way of saying equal pay for work of equal value. I think it is a good concept. Some of the recent reports recognize the reality that women will continue mainly to do women's work, but that women's work has been historically grossly undervalued and, therefore, should be much better paid. While we must make every effort to help women break into the traditional male jobs, it will be very difficult because it seems that our society is not set up to handle two-career families who must raise children at the same time. A sacrifice must be made and as a result of role conditioning and biology, to some extent, it is usually the woman who must make the sacrifice. Indeed, househusbands are rare.
Child rearing must be recognized as valuable labour in order to give women economic strength. Surely, parenting is the most important job in the world. Imagine a society which paid
Employment Equity
mothers the same amount as corporation presidents. That is not likely to happen but the difference between what mothers are paid-usually nothing-and what we pay corporate presidents shows how undervalued parenting is in our society. Parenting is a low status job and society must change its values in this regard.
The job of a Member of Parliament can only be carried out if that Member has a support person to look after the children and other household responsibilities. It is a job that is more easily carried out by a single person. One can see that a disproportionate number of women in the House of Commons are single or have no children. Of 282 Members of Parliament, only 28 are women, or 9.6 per cent. Of 39 chiefs of staff, only 4, or 10.3 per cent, are women.
The reason for this is that men have wives to look after the children. The problem is that the reverse does not occur. The real solution is not to have more househusbands but to provide for more work-sharing and to place a high value on child care so that families who choose to have children are not discriminated against economically in the workplace. For example, women who work in a law firm should not be forced to fit into the male mould but should have an equal footing with men. In this way, men will be just as interested in looking after the children after work rather than staying late to work on a case.
Employment equity is beneficial because it promotes women in the workplace and promotes equal pay for work of equal value. Placing a higher value on women's work gives women more economic strength. It lowers the barriers in job ghettos so as to make traditional women's work more financially attractive to men, thereby equalizing sex roles in our society.
I repeat that this Bill is inadequate because there is no enforcement mechanism. It is not sufficient to rely on a reporting system. The Bill must have more strength in order for it to work. That is why I commend to the House some of the suggestions made by my Party as well as some of the suggestions made by the United Chinese Community Services Society in Vancouver. I look forward to seeing some of those suggestions implemented.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate. In fact. Bill C-62, which is aimed at legislating employment equity, arises from a private Member's Bill.
Mr. Speaker, as we all know, the House is considering a motion to suspend consideration of the Bill and resume debate in six months' time, in other to give the Government a chance to reconsider and make the necessary changes.
Mr. Speaker, on the face of it, as far as the principle of the Bill is concerned, I do not think anyone in the House is against employment equity. It is a principle we accept and which we want to support. It is a principle that commands respect, and in any case, it is high time it was put into practice.

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
However, Bill C-62 now before the House is a clumsy and extremely ill-planned piece of legislation, drafted with ... It is almost amateurish, Mr. Speaker, and I am sorry to have to say this, but any Member of Parliament, upon reading the Bill over, will say it is not only ambiguous but is often so difficult to understand that it undermines the very objective and principle of the Bill itself.
Hon. Members will recall that Bill C-62 supports the hiring of women, native people, handicapped persons and persons whose race or colour make them members of what we refer to as Canada's visible minorities. To reach its objective, Bill C-62 is proposing to eliminate employment barriers. It also proposes to provide for fair proportional representation of members of these groups in various jobs, and I quote Clause 4 (b):
(i)	in the work force, or
(ii)	in those segments of the work force that are identifiable by qualification, eligibility or geography and from which the employer may reasonably be expected to draw or promote employees.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-62 proposes that every year, starting on or before June 1988, every employer shall file with the Minister of Employment and Immigration a report providing a profile of the employer's employees, an annual report that will be tabled in Parliament. That is in the Bill.
Upon summary conviction, if the employer concerned fails to comply with the legislation and does not file this report, he will be liable to a fine not exceeding $50,000. And speaking of employers, Mr. Speaker, these are federal enterprises with 100 employees or more, and any corporate entity employing 100 or more employees on, or in connection with, a federal work or undertaking or business.
The exception, Mr. Speaker-I realize I do not have much time left, but I do want to raise this particular point- departments are excluded under the provisions of Sections 2 of the Financial Administration Act. When we examine this Bill and read that Departments are excluded under the provisions of the Financial Administration Act, we say to ourselves: Well of course, because several years ago, Treasury Board introduced an affirmative action program which, I think, reflects the intentions of the previous Liberal Government to set an example, at least with its own employees. So, in Bill C-62, departments are excluded. If we try and find out what is a department-

When we try to find out how that is defined, we look at the Financial Administration Act and note that those subject to Schedule 1 and Schedule 2 are exempted because they are covered by Treasury Board, which is the employer.
However, if one looks at others which may be Crown corporations or companies which have a mandate from Parliament, one finds that those are not covered by Bill C-62, nor by the Financial Administration Act.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-EFFECT OF CHANGE IN UNION REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the House the Government's neglect in dealing with the concerns of those employees of Canadian National whose rights to union representation have been violated.
More than six months ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) became aware that 50 Ontario workers were in limbo because of a change in union membership from the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers to the Teamsters. These 50 workers were even denied the right to vote, and have been told that they have lost their right to seniority for modified jobs within the Canadian Brotherhood, and have further been denied representation by the Teamsters.
Workers like David Malcolmson and Henry Singleton of Hamilton have a combined service of 27 years with Canadian National, and have been told to quit their jobs and reapply in the normal fashion so they might be able to find modified work or to find the door.
When we inquired on their behalf, we were told to write a letter to the Minister. The Minister has had a letter on this subject for more than six months. David Malcolmson is about to lose his job because he remains in a state of limbo caused by the Government's inaction.
I call on the Minister of Transport to resolve this problem immediately and save the jobs of Canadian workers. These workers rightfully deserve better treatment. They deserve action on the part of the Minister of Transport, not letters and inaction.

subtopic: TWENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF SAINTE-ANNE-DE-BELLEVUE ARCTIC BIOLOGICAL STATION
TWENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF SAINTE-ANNE-DE-BELLEVUE ARCTIC BIOLOGICAL STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last weekend, the Arctic Biological Station at Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue, in the riding of Vaudreuil, celebrated its 20th anniversary. In fact, we could even say its 40th anniversary, since the origins of this institution go back to 1946, thanks to the efforts of Professor Max Dunbar of McGill University.
Mr. Speaker, the Arctic Biological Station is unique in this country. Over the years, the station has received international recognition for its work, and there is no other institution like it in Canada, especially if we consider the expertise of its staff, its specialized library and its location.

The Saint-Anne Arctic Biological Station, Mr. Speaker, has the mandate to study Arctic marine life. The importance of this mandate becomes abundantly clear when one realizes that
90 per cent of all Canadian waters are either Arctic or sub-Arctic.
In addition, current projections estimate that for the remainder of the 1980s and through the 1990s, 25 per cent of all major Canadian capital projects will be in our North. [Translation]
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add that the excellent work done by all those either directly or indirectly concerned with the activities of the Station over the years deserved to be mentioned here in the House, and that we shall watch with interest as they continue in their quest to increase our knowledge and understanding of Canada's North.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO PLANNED PARENTHOOD ORGANIZATION S
OBJECTION TO PLANNED PARENTHOOD ORGANIZATION S
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been concern recently about funding levels for Planned Parenthood, both nationally and at the provincial level in Saskatchewan.
As one who supports the principle of public education on family planning and birth control, I agree with the general objectives of an organization like Planned Parenthood. However, there is one very objectionable aspect of Planned Parenthood's philosophy that cannot be tolerated by people of conscience. It is Planned Parenthood's stand on abortion.
Regardless of one's view on the subject, abortion is prohibited in the Criminal Code, except under certain circumstances. Yet Planned Parenthood continues to counsel that abortion is an equal alternative to women facing the birth of a child.
Planned Parenthood counsellors are instructed to state that an expectant woman has three options: carry a child to term and retain custody, place the child for adoption, or have an abortion. By doing this, Planned Parenthood is openly promoting an act which is illegal. Further, this counselling relegates Planned Parenthood to the role of an abortion referral agency.
I join with millions of Canadian taxpayers who feel that their tax dollars might be used for birth control information, but must not be used for the promotion of abortion.

speechtext:

20.000	jobs in the shoe industry for the sole purpose of increasing the profits of a few big retail importers.

6.000	more jobs and fully safeguarding the interests of the consumer. No quotas means these jobs will disappear and increased profits for a few big retail importers.

Mr. Speaker, there are some things that take place in this House that drive one to distraction, even to the point of using unparliamentary language.
In over 20 years the most direct action the Liberal Government took in relation to the environment was a former Prime Minister writing a letter to a local Liberal candidate stating that he would urge the United States authorities to stop polluting the Niagara River. If he had been serious about the concerns of those millions of people living within the Niagara River-Great Lakes basin, instead of writing about it now, he would have then improved the Canada-U.S. Water Quality Agreement; he would have then joined with the provincial Government in taking legal action against U.S. polluters; and he sould have then been working with the people in the municipalities of Niagara to fund the elimination of Canadian pollutants. subtopic: PENSION PLAN REVISIONS-PLEA ON BEHALF OF PRESENT SUPERANNUATES
PENSION PLAN REVISIONS-PLEA ON BEHALF OF PRESENT SUPERANNUATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in April of this year the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) announced that an agreement had been reached with the unions representing Public Service employees on the principles to govern the introduction of pension plan revisions. Both the Government and the unions agreed that Public Service pension plans would be funded and administered in accordance with accepted practices of major private-sector employers.
This means that current indexing of pensions would be replaced by an inflation protection feature based upon the earnings of the fund. Placing Public Service pension arrangements on a sound financial basis is a proposal with much merit.

my constituency on June 21 this year. 1 now state it again. My stand on this issue has not changed.

They are appealing to us to be their voice in reversing a decision which is both unjust and unfair.

I ask all Hon. Members to protest and insist that CP Rail squelch this policy which punishes its pensioners.

subsubtopic: FUTURE LEVELS OF IMMIGRATION-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE (IMMIGRATION)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to indicate that the Government is today signalling that Canada is once again welcoming immigrants. [Translation]
Today the Government reiterates its intention of welcoming immigrants.

I have tabled in the House the report on future immigration levels for the next two calendar years. Immigration levels are being increased to 105,000 to 115,000 in 1986 and 115,000 to
125,000	in 1987. This is up from the 85,000 to 90,000 announced for 1985. The Government believes that, contrary to myths, immigrants do not take jobs away from Canadians but instead contribute positively to our economic and social development. This view has been confirmed by comprehensive consultations undertaken this year, by reports of the parliamentary Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, and by the recent report of the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects.
The two-year plan announced today represents a new era for immigration policy and stresses the postive longer term impact of the program. During this period, the level will be rebuilt in a moderate, controlled manner which will, in a balanced way, support the reunion of families, the admission of humanitarian immigrants and the selection of economic immigrants. Taken as a whole, this plan will place the immigration program back on the path of the more traditional and widely accepted post-war levels.
Taken as a whole this plan will place the immigration program back on the path of the more traditional and widely accepted post-war levels.

Specifically, the Government will be implementing the policy through its major programs.
First, family class. The family class will remain the cornerstone of immigration policy, and we will continue to process applications on demand.

The family class will remain the cornerstone of immigration policy, and we will continue to process applications on demand.

Government projections suggest that 45,000 landings may occur next year. But I want to stress that this is not a quota or a ceiling, and this projection may be exceeded if demand rises.
October 31, 1985

Second, the humanitarian program. Canada will increase its growth of Government assisted refugees in 1986 by 1,000 from
11,000	to 12,000. This is at a time when many refugee receiving nations are becoming more restrictive.

Canada will increase its growth of Government assisted refugees in 1986 from 11,000 to 12,000. This at a time when many refugees receiving nations are becoming more restrictive. [English]
These refugees will be aided by an additional provision of $3 million to the Adjustment Assistance Program. An additional $750,000 is being provided to agencies to provide direct aid to refugees and other needy immigrants. In total, the 1986 plan allows for some 20,000 to 23,000 humanitarian landings, the second largest plan in the world next to the United States.

The creation of a new investors program will encourage immigration of business people with proven track records, who have resources to invest in Canada. This new program will directly support the efforts of Investment Canada.
Statements by Ministers
These changes represent an important first step in revitalizing the immigration program on a longer term basis. They recognize the important contribution that immigrants make to national economic development. This rationale was easily understood by our forebears but it has been all too quickly forgotten in an era when we have become overly preoccupied in solving our short-term problems. The Government is committed to a longer term role for immigration and, as the Minister responsible, I intend to engage Canadians in a dialogue to develop the next steps of this program.

The Government is committed to a longer term role for immigration and, as Minister responsible, I intend to engage Canadians in a dialogue to develop the next steps of this program.

We may need to consider in the next two years significantly higher levels of immigration if we are to sustain our population growth and economic development.
Today, the Government has presented a plan which will restore the balance among the major immigration themes in a moderate, controlled way. It will also be conducting a demographic review under the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). We will be closely monitoring these changes to ensure their effectiveness and, if needed, I will bring further revisions to the House next fall.
I trust all Members of the House will join with me in supporting these positive changes, which the Government is introducing today. Canada is sending a message world-wide that from now on this country will be welcoming more immigrants to support its longer term economic and social goals.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to welcome this report to the extent that it does increase our immigration levels in the areas that are needed, to a small extent. It is a very small extent. As the Minister knows, because of the studies done this year with the aid of his Department and through the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, the figure he quotes is nowhere near enough even to maintain the existing population level of Canada. We would need between 150,000 and 175,000 just to stay where we are, according to the information received by the parliamentary committee and tabled this spring. However, granted, it is a move in the right direction, and the Minister says that there will be further moves in other years, which is also encouraging, although it is unnecessarily slow for the reasons I will point out.
The category of families and the category of assisted relatives are being unnecessarily held back by the practices of the Employment and Immigration Commission. They are being held back in three ways. One is that excessively high incomes are demanded of Canadians who wish to bring over, to sponsor an assisted relative. During the past year when the cost of living went up 4 per cent, the amount of income required of a sponsoring relative here went up 9 per cent. This was similar to increases in previous years, but this is the one for which the Minister's Government is responsible, and I think it is very regrettable.
There is also the matter of the visa offices which are very poorly distributed in the countries from which many of our immigrants come, and it takes sometimes years to process an application because there is one office for India, two offices for all of Africa, two offices for all of Central America, and those have to go through Trinidad. The third way it is limited is that the health and welfare requirements are becoming more and more nit-picking. When a whole family is kept out because a 12-year old child has a speech impediment, then it is clear that it is something that happens to Third World immigrants and would not happen to somebody from my old country, that is to say, Great Britain.
The figures are royally confusing because the Minister's figures do not jibe with the figures in the report which was distributed about five minutes ago. Apparently he has only
selected some of the items, but they are also confusing because of their comparison with the report of a year ago. He has implied that there might be an increase-he has not stated it-in the family class. In fact, there is no increase. He has given a figure for refugees and humanitarian immigration which is, at maximum, 23,000, the same as the maximum for last year. There is no increased for family immigration, no increase for refugees, members of designated classes and people who are landed under special humanitarian measures.
There is an increase for selected workers, principal applicants and their spouses and dependents. That is where the main increase comes. That is nearly doubled from about
13,000	last year to perhaps-it is more than doubled-13,000, depending on which figures one uses, to about twice that or a little more for this year. Then there is a doubling-more than a doubling, really-of the figures for business immigrants. No, perhaps it is not more than a doubling-I just had these figures a few minutes ago-but they are up from 7,000, including the families, to 12,000 now.
The Minister's figures given in his statement would total
97,000.	The figures in his report total 105,000 to 115,000, so I do hope the Minister will disregard his statement and act according to his report, and I do hope he understands that there has been no increase in humanitarian immigration this year.
I have one further point, and that is, I welcome the statement by the Minister that there will be an increase of, I think it is, $3 million in the Adjustment Assistance Program. This is long overdue and very welcome. He also says there will be $750,000 to agencies providing direct aid to refugees. I hope that will cure some of the difficulties now provided by lack of counsel to immigrants arriving at Toronto and Montreal.
All in all, the improvements are very small, most of them are in the right direction, and we hope that they indicate that the administration of immigration will be much more humane in the coming year.

speechtext:
Our achievements have been of historic significance. Our first step toward market-sensitive pricing came last November when we lifted restrictions on the sale of Canadian natural gas in international markets. This step increased our volume of natural gas exports in the current gas year by 23 per cent and increased our share of the important U.S. market. That was our first step toward removing Government from the natural gas market-place.
Statements by Ministers
Our next step was the deregulation of oil prices on June 1 under the terms of the Western Accord. We promised to let industry get on with the job of exploring, producing and selling its product.
The agreement which I am tabling today completes the task we imposed on ourselves. Canada and the producing provinces have reached an agreement which is fair to both consumers and producers. We expect the agreement to have favourable regional and national effects on investment, employment and trade.
For the first time in a decade, all Canadians should benefit from an industry which is free of unnecessary Government intervention and is responsive to market conditions. Consumers will have freer access to supplies, and producers will have freer access to both domestic and international markets.
Because of complexities such as existing contractual arrangements in moving to a market-oriented pricing system, the agreement provides for a one-year transition period between the old regime and the new. This agreement is an excellent example of balanced compromise in the national interest.
During a transition period between tomorrow, which is the start of the new gas year, and November 1, 1986, the cost of natural gas will be frozen at both the Alberta border price and the Toronto wholesale price. As markets adjust to our new regime, the Alberta border price will remain at $2.79 per gigajoule, and the Toronto wholesale price will be frozen at its current level of $3.79 per gigajoule, which includes the costs of transportation from Alberta.
The price freeze at the wholesale level will mean that price levels for eastern Canadian consumers should decline as distributors pass on benefits provided to them through provisions contained in the Western Accord. Residential consumers will pay lower gas costs this winter than last as they benefit from the removal of the Canadian ownership charge of 8 cents per gigajoule due to be applied on November 1.
Under our new gas agreement, further benefits should result to consumers as producers, absorb the November 1 rise in the TransCanada Pipelines' transportation toll for the transition period. This was an important contribution by the producers which will benefit consumers. In return, the producers will get increased access to export markets.

In addition, arrangements have been made to provide equitable access for British Columbia gas through the Alberta pipeline system to new markets both in the U.S. and eastern Canada. As a Minister from British Columbia, I must say that that gives my province enormous opportunities. Similarly, the agreement leaves room for consuming provinces such as Quebec to deal with regulatory issues that are within provincial jurisdiction. speechtext:
That is right, about an hour ago. I will do my best to respond to it in short detail.
First, I want to explain to Canadians generally how important natural gas is. I suppose it is only Canadians who could feel that this is a fundamental debate. However, it is in Canada because next to oil natural gas in Canada's most important fuel. There has been a growth in its use to 25 per cent in the three decades since the trans-Canada pipeline was built to bring gas from western Canada to the East. By the year 2005 gas will catch up with oil as Canada's top home heating, cooking, industrial and transportation fuel. We will even be fueling some of our cars with natural gas. The National Energy Board estimates that oil and gas will each fill 31 per cent of Canada's energy needs in the year 2005. That is quite incredible, which is why this measure is so important. What we are discussing today may be the policy for the next decade.
On top of that, we are seeing a tremendous growth, according to Oilweek magazine, of gas exports to the United States. Somewhere between 15 per cent and 22 per cent of our production is exported. I would ask Members of the House to keep that in mind as we discuss this document today.
I can sum it up this way, Mr. Speaker. The mountain has laboured and brought forward a mouse. After a year of different committees, meetings of different groups, a year of consideration, this is what has been brought forward. If one looks at this document one will see that it is all shoulds, all reviews-it is all fudge. In effect, there is no real deregulation at all if one really looks at it. Perhaps it is impossible to deregulate the gas market because it is such a complicated one. It is much more complicated than oil.
However, the fact is that there is not much deregulation here. As a matter of fact, there is a retention of monopolistic practices by gas distribution Firms, the established intermediaries in the market which have exclusive rights of sales and services. They have long-standing regional franchises and contracts. There has been no effort to break up TransCanada Pipelines, the monopolistic carrier, which really could have brought lower prices for eastern consumers rather than fudging it with an announcement that the producers will absorb the recent increase in the transportation costs.

The Minister says there should be no intervention in the market-place. That is nonsense. Of course, there is intervention in the market-place. There are decisions with respect to exports. a holding action for about a year. That is what I see in this agreement. The Minister says on page 3 that the price levels for eastern consumers should decline as distributors pass on benefits. I have two comments to make on that. The Minister says: "should". I prefer "will". Let's have some guarantees that they will decline. After all, if we go by the market-as I am constantly told by the Conservative Members opposite and all around me-if we have a surplus then prices, it seems to me, should decline. They should and they would decline, but here we are dealing with simply a hope that they may decline. Prices would decline in a free market but we are just hoping they may decline.
There is something else which causes me problems. Were we not promised this with the Western Accord? Were we not going to have declining oil prices? Were not the consumers going to benefit? speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking once again to Bill C-62, I just want to say that although I agree with the principle of the Bill, I am against buying a "pig in a poke". The Bill's substance is weak, its presentation is clumsy, it is poorly drafted, and I think it should go back to the drawing board and be redone and re-thought and submitted again to the House, so that we can then adopt a Bill that is truly positive and constructive. Mr. Speaker, that is why I am glad of this chance to speak to the motion to postpone adoption of the Bill for six months, so as to give the Government a chance to reconsider, re-think and re-draft the Bill.
Mr. Speaker, I just want to discuss a few provisions of the Bill which are basically quite valid but which are poorly defined and as such unsatisfactory. In the Bill it says that the purpose is to give Canadians who suffer some form of discrimination, the right to be hired by Canadian employers, whether they are handicapped, aboriginal peoples, women or, as it says in the Bill, people who because of their race or colour, the so-called visible minorities, have until now been discriminated against.
Mr. Speaker, the Bill does not define these terms. It does not say what an aboriginal person is, but Hon. Members will recall that Section 35(2) of the Canadian Constitution gives a very clear definition of what "aboriginal person" means. So what definition are we to use when we read this Bill? I really do not know. And if we consider the handicapped, for instance, how should we define a handicapped person? Is it someone who wears glasses, like me, or someone who wears a hearing aid, like you, Mr. Speaker, or is it someone who by definition should be recognized as having a physical problem, some kind of difficulty, a handicap that prevents him from finding a job? I think the program we had under the previous Liberal Government, set up by Treasury Board for federal employees, is an excellent program, an affirmative action program for hiring handicapped persons. I think we could agree on something like that. The Government could call Mrs. Suzanne Azzie at the Public Service Commission, for instance, and she could explain, Mr. Speaker, what she is doing at the Commission to promote and support the hiring of handicapped persons. I think that we would get a far more appropriate and a fairer and more precise definition.
Adjournment Motion
Mr. Speaker, the Bill also covers people suffering from congenital or acquired deficiencies and mental or physical disabilities which prevent them from working normally. Well, Mr. Speaker, I ask the Government to give us a clear and specific definition of a handicapped person.
I said so and again I repeat that the Bill is ill-defined and restrictive. For instance, why is there no reference to the various religious groups? Are they not entitled as well to employment equity? Clause 3 of the Bill excludes departments as defined in the Financial Administration Act, federal departments are excluded, the House of Commons is excluded, the Senate is excluded, separate employers are excluded. I appreciate that the Treasury Board has a good law, a good regulation concerning affirmative action, but I wonder how a Minister can be excluded under this Bill C-62 which does not come under the Treasury Board because it is not an employer, how anyone is justified to tell the House: Pass a piece of legislation, but as a Minister you will have to exclude me. Mr. Speaker, I find it totally unacceptable that a Minister would come to the House without being able to give us a more serious and more reasonable argument in favour of this Bill.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of Crown corporations and a good many important agencies which are excluded under Bill C-62, they are not covered under the affirmative action program proposed in Bill C-62.
Mr. Speaker, I see that you are getting impatient and prepared to cut me off, but I would simply like to say that some of the provisions of this Bill are unacceptable. We will vote against the Bill, not because the principle is bad, on the contrary, but the Bill is deficient. We simply cannot support this Bill, Mr. Speaker.

I guess we should not reflect on a decision made by the Chair. I want to say a few words on the motion before the House, specifically, a motion for a six-month hoist. I want to direct my comments specifically to why I support the idea of delaying the Bill for an extra six months. Bill C-62 supposedly would provide for employment equity for four target groups in our society; namely, women, the native people of Canada, visible minorities and Canadians who are disabled. We have heard from organizations representing all these groups. They are all saying that even though they like the idea of Parliament talking about employment equity, the problem is that the Bill before the House is strictly a voluntary measure. A voluntary measure is not good enough to ensure employment equity, Mr. Speaker. We need mandatory action. I have copies of various statements made by organizations representing the four target groups. They are all telling us that we need mandatory affirmative action. They are telling us that good sentiments and voluntary measures are not enough, that we need targets, goals, specific action and timetabling by the Government of Canada.
For that reason the Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) this morning moved a motion for a six-month hoist. He said that Conservative Members of Parliament need an extra six months to think this over. I am pleased to see the Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) in the House. He chaired a subcommittee on equality in recent months and did a superb job, along with the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), a Member of the Liberal Party and other Members of his Party. After a great deal of work they issued a unanimous report along with recommendations to the House of Commons on equality.
One of their comments was that Bill C-62, introduced by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), was not adequate. They said that rather than leaving this strive for equality to the goodwill of Government and big business, mandatory rules, laws and regulations were needed in this country. I commend the chairman of the subcommittee for that recommendation.
By moving this motion for a six-month hoist, we are helping the Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore to persuade his colleagues that the Bill must be changed. We are helping him persuade his colleagues that they must listen to native Canadians, to women, to the disabled and visible minorities in this country who need specific goals, targets and mandatory action to provide equality in the workplace. That is why we have moved this motion for a six-month hoist. I know that you and many Members of the Conservative Party are intelligent and can understand this quickly but there are many Members of that Party who need another six months to catch up to the Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore and the subcommittee in order to understand what these four target groups are saying about this Bill.
I appeal to Canadians to telephone their local Member of Parliament in the Conservative Party and ask them to support this motion to delay the Bill an extra six months so that the Minister of Employment and Immigration can introduce a new Bill that reflects the four groups in society whom this Bill is supposed to help. That is specifically what we are debating this afternoon and specifically the reason why we are attempting to delay this piece of legislation for an extra six months. I wish we were dealing now with a Bill that those people want and could pass it quickly so that we could make sure there is equity in this country. However, that is not the case with the Bill before us.
I will not go through the statistics again relating to discrimination against women in this country and the fact that their pensions and salaries are much lower than those of men. We know that their opportunity for advancement is much lower than that of men. In this very House of Commons, there are only 28 female Members of Parliament and well over 250 male Members of Parliament. There is great inequality even in this Chamber. There are very few female chiefs of staff of cabinet Ministers. There are very few women who have important functions in the Public Service.

The Minister of National Health and Welfare says: "We are". I recall some courageous stands he has taken and that is a reason why he is a prominent cabinet Minister. I want to see other Conservative Members of Parliament have the courage of their convictions and take a stand to fight for real equality in this country. In that way they will back up the Minister of Health and Parliament will have the kind of Bill that is demanded by women, native people, visible minorities and disabled Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you agree with this position and I know that a lot of Progressive Conservative members do too. But, unfortunately, they are all scared of the Prime Minister, even those representing Quebec ridings . .. They are all scared. [English]
However, they should not forget what happens to a backbencher who is afraid to speak out. We saw what happened to Liberals when they lost in the 1984 election.

You are holding your hands like you are about to pray, Mr. Speaker. 1 agree with you. That is why we were elected and I invite my friends in the Conservative Party to take that stand now. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is tough, sometimes vindictive, sometimes very unfair and he may by-pass some of those Members for a Cabinet position. However, that is not the most important thing in life. It is more important for those Members to say what they believe and represent their constituents. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I heard the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) speak about fairness, equality and equity. I would suggest that he did not have that in mind in his reference to the Prime Minister. I am sure he understands that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret that the Hon. Member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) stood up to talk about equity and fairness. I am glad we are talking about a Bill dealing with employment equity because we want to remind the Minister of Labour that the federal minimum wage is $3.50 an hour. The minimum wage in all of the provinces is more than $3.50 an hour. In fact, the difference is some provinces is a dollar an hour.
When talking about employment equity and equal pay for work of equal value, the Minister should listen because someone can be working for a federal Government Department in Ottawa on one floor, making $3.50 an hour, and the next day go to the next floor to work for a private enterprise or the provincial Government and make $4 an hour. In another province, you could make $3.50 an hour on federal property under the Canada Labour Code, on any contract that is awarded. You could have minimum wage for doing the same work one week and about a dollar an hour less for doing exactly the same job the next week.
In your province does an MLA get the same salary as yours?

I just bring that to the attention of the House because the difference is getting greater.
