Employment Equity
A provincial Member in Newfoundland is paid less than you are.
I did not hear the Hon. Member.
Oh, oh!

The Hon. Member, 1 presume, is in favour of a low minimum wage for the federal Government and a higher minimum wage for the provincial administration. When you talk about equal pay for work of equal value, Mr. Speaker, it is a very important point for the Minister of Labour to keep in mind.
Let me get back to the Bill, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

The Bill before the Chamber is flawed in certain areas. We have the Government of Canada saying it is bringing in a Bill to force employers to hire women and to hire people in the other designated groups. That is what the Governmenmt is saying. That is what the Minister said in her speech when she introduced the Bill. Then you have the Opposition saying that the Bill does not go far enough.
What is the truth in the Bill, Mr. Speaker? I had a look at the Bill a moment ago to see what was in it. I suppose the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) is correct when he says that the Bill is perhaps poorly drafted. I would not say that exactly, Mr. Speaker, because drafting of a Bill is a very specialized field of work. People who draft legislation are specialized people. We in Canada have some of the best drafters of legislation. Years ago provincial administrations had to bring people from Britain or Scotland just to fulfil those functions. What you give the drafter to put in the legislation is the problem. How can you be specific and write a law that a judge is going to look at and give the proper interpretation to, saying that this was the intention of Parliament when it passed that law?
Some things are quite obvious in the Bill, as the Hon. Member pointed out. The Bill excludes "Department" as defined under the Financial Administration Act. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that when you look at the Financial Administration Act and you look at "Department", it does not define Government "Department". That is a part of the definition, yes, in Schedule A, but you have Schedule B and Schedule C which are not Government Departments at all. The definition of Department comes under the Financial Administration Act. As the Member for Ottawa Vanier pointed out, it excludes the House of Commons, the Senate, commissions of inquiry and all kinds of agencies of the federal Government. That is not a flaw by the drafter. That is what was fed into the Bill by the Department, I believe, intentionally.
The important clause and the important words are "that the various positions of employment with the employer are proportionate to the representation in the workforce or in segments of the workforce. If you have a law, Mr. Speaker, which says that you must hire proportionate to, then the numbers never
change, do they? In other words, if you have B.C. Tel hiring telephone operators and its percentage of women is 90 per cent hiring and B.C. Tel is going on an average of Bell Telephone which is 99 per cent average, then B.C. Tel would feel when it looked at this Bill that it would have to hire more women.
If Bell were hiring the women and the situation were reversed, that the average number of women was more than it had, the company would have to say: "To comply with this legislation, we have to hire less women as telephone operators". Do you get my point, Mr. Speaker? It is a very important point.
What should be inserted there to satisfy the Minister's demands is that: "it is at least proportionate to" a percentage of their representation. I do not think this is the fault of the drafter, but I think some of it is actual intent.
One section says that the Minister "may" issue guidelines. The Minister demands of an employer that you have to do this, that or something else, but you do not then turn around and say the Minister "may" issue some guidelines to the employer. What is the employer supposed to do? He has this Bill and he says "I have to comply with this Bill. I have a contract from Supply and Services." The Government better listen to this because it is important. What if you have a contract from Supply and Services and your first clause in the contract is that you must abide by all laws and regulations of the federal Government and the provincial Government where the work is being carried out? If this is the law, a person has to look at it and say: "What am I supposed to do? To whom am 1 supposed to go to get the information on the number of women to hire and the number of people in the other categories? The word should not be that the Minister may issue guidelines directed to employers. It should be that she must issue.
There are other mistakes in the Bill, such as the occupational groups of the employer and the degree of representation of persons in the designated groups in each occupational group- the occupational groups of the employees, not the employer. There are obvious small errors in the Bill, perhaps some of them typographical.
Let me get back to the Minister of Labour and the minimum wage when you list salary differences and so on. I believe the federal legislation on the minimum wage is in the regulation. It states that it should approximate the provincial minimum wage as an understanding, which it presently does not. I know what the Minister is talking about. I have been searching for something, and I think I have found it in the general guidelines. It says the federal Government should have increased the minimum wage. The Liberal Government always did prior to that, Mr. Speaker. It always did, but the Conservatives do not.
I have one minute left, so let me tell the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) that the most discriminatory rules and regulations as they relate to employment are in the Minister's own direct employment programs in the federal Government this year. For example, you have to be out of work 24 of the previous 30 weeks to get work in the biggest employment program of this Minister.
October 31, 1985

That excludes all students coming out of school, all new entrants and all re-entrants. If a woman is out of the workforce for a year trying to get back in, she has not been unemployed for 30 months because she has not been registered for employment. It excludes people who actually work seven weeks for the previous seven months.
When you talk about equity in employment, Mr. Speaker, equity means fairness. I suppose any dictionary would say that. The Minister should look right in her own back yard and see how unfair she is being to people who want jobs and want training programs in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to support the very wise motion to delay this Bill. It is very important that there be a redraft of the Bill so we can all support employment equity in the real sense and have it implemented and enforced in a way that will not only be possible within designated companies but within society as a whole.
The New Democratic Party cannot support the Bill as it is because we believe it will not achieve the goals we all desire. We all want women, minority groups, native people and disabled persons to have equal opportunities in the workplace to get a job in the first place, and equal opportunities to have decent rates of pay, equal pay for work of equal value, to training opportunities and promotions. We are concerned that there is not the enforcement mechanism in the Bill as it stands now to achieve this important goal.
Experience has shown that voluntary affirmative action, which is really what the Bill is advocating, will not achieve this goal. I refer particularly to a study of affirmative action in Canada called Ten Years After. It was a summary prepared by the Department of the Secretary of State. The consultant who prepared the report said that voluntary affirmative action had not worked and that the observable and measureable results after 10 years must be classed as disappointing. This was a study of voluntary affirmative action in the provinces of Canada and in the federal Government to date. Surely the Conservatives do not want to be the same as the Liberals, and just leave this to chance.
Hear, hear!

That is what you are really doing. The Conservatives are suggesting a voluntary kind of employment equity. Changing the name does not change the nature of it, and we are very concerned.
To those colleagues who are in support of business, I want to say that the heads of a number of notable corporations in the United States have supported mandatory affirmative action. They have not done it just because they feel it is better for their employees, but because they have found, through experience, that it is productive and gives economic results within their companies. Let us not have any more of this hog-wash about being afraid to make the business community conform.
Employment Equity
That is my line.

We are not dealing with hogs; we are dealing with employment equity.
We are opposed to the Bill in principle because it is based upon voluntary employment equity rather than mandatory employment equity. As I said before, employers are not required to impose clear goals, targets and timetables for change. Only record keeping is required, not necessarily change. There is no independent enforcement agency named which can really do a job in establishing what changes are needed in given corporations and in enforcing them. There are no sanctions for compliance. Also there is no reference to equal pay for work of equal value. That is a very significant omission.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission has been named-and the Minister has referred to this several times- as the agency which would evaluate programs and take individual complaints from employees. I want to stress again that the problem with that is that it is individual complaints. It is up to a woman somehow to find the resources to document here case, endanger her job, obtain the necessary information and go to the Human Rights Commission if she has a complaint. That is not the way it should be. It should be systemic change. It should be built into the system what changes are necessary to make employment equal in a given field or place of employment.
Also I should like to point out that this will place an impossible load upon an already overloaded Human Rights Commission. I have referred to an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on October 30 by Michael Harris indicating that there was a two-year backlog in the work-load of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. Also it indicated that the backlog was caused by heavy work-load and staff changes. Last spring the Minister said in the House that she would make extra resources available and that the commission would be able to deal with these matters. It is six months later, and it still has a two-year backlog. There is no way the commission can take on the extra load expected in the Bill. Even if it did, it does not have the power to enforce, as I have already said.
I should like to refer to the recently tabled report Equality for All of the Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights. It contains a very detailed section on employment equity. The Bill was out when the committee looked at the matter. Unfortunately I do not have the time to refer to all its recommendations, but quite a number of improvements were recommended. It would only make sense to take the time to look at these, to have another look at the Bill and to try to redraft it so that it will get at these things. I should like to mention two or three points which I feel are particularly important. Recommendation No. 61 reads:
We recommend that representatives of the appropriate designated groups (women, underrepresented visible minorities, native peoples and disabled people) be involved ... with management and labour in developing employment equity programs.
There is nothing in the Bill about that or about collective bargaining. Recommendation No. 62 reads:

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
We recommend that legislation on employment equity contain enforcement mechanisms providing for the review of special programs by the Canadian Human Rights Commission, and that the Commission be given additional financial and human resources for this purpose.
1 have just referred to how inadequate we are in that area. Recommendation No. 63 reads:
We recommend that, to assure employment equity, a contract compliance program be established by legislation and that it apply to all firms providing goods and services to the Government of Canada-
There is no contract compliance in the Bill. Recommendation No. 66 reads:
We recommend that federal training and education programs be made accessible to women, disabled people, native people and members of underrepresented visible minorities to assist in achieving employment equity.
There is no reference to that in the Bill. We know that the Abella Commission strongly recommended training opportunities so that people in disadvantaged groups could move into jobs and upward in an equal way.
I am rushing because I want to put several recommendations on the record. I should like to refer to a group in Vancouver East, the United Chinese Community Enrichment Services Society, an agency which is particularly concerned with services and advocacy for Chinese Canadian people in Vancouver, and indeed in the province. It has reviewed the Bill very carefully, as it always does, and the chairperson, Sandra Wilking, recommended the following:
We agree with the spirit of the legislation. However, we would like the Legislative Review Committee to reconsider the following areas... (1) The possibility of expanding the definition of "designated groups" to include "minorities-
These are not necessarily visible minorities. That is a very interesting point. I do not think many of us have considered it. She continued by indicating, for example, that people from Mediterranean and Latin American backgrounds who do not speak English face considerable discrimination in the workplace and that they should be included. I think it was particularly sensitive to suggest an expansion of the groups which should be included.
Her second point on behalf of the society referred to including unions in the employer group which falls under federal jurisdiction for example, that the Public Service Alliance, which is responsible for employing quite a number of staff, should be considered in this employment equity jurisdiction. That was another sensible point. Her third recommendation was:
We are concerned that the current proposed legislation remains silent on the enforcement factor. Who will be responsible for ensuring that there are positive results toward employment equity in the employer group? Who will police the Act?
That is a very good question. She continued:
The fine of $5,000 is not as efficient as specific performance and other remedies.
I see your signal, Mr. Speaker. Her fourth point was that the Bill was not clear on what types of relevant data would be required in employers' reports. Her fifth point was that if employers were to recruit for various target groups, they should look at the ethnicity question. It is very interesting that
this visible minority group would suggest that Anglo-Saxons be included as an ethnic group to be considered. Perhaps we Anglo-Saxons are very patronizing in what we think of as the majority, which perhaps is the minority. We tend to think that we are not ethnic, that everyone else is ethnic.
I ask that these matters be referred to committee for consideration. I urge all Hon. Members of the House, particularly Conservative Members who have the power to make changes, if they would only use it, to consider seriously a delay in the Bill and trying to improve it so that there will be true equality for women and minority groups in employment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion which would have the effect of sending this Bill back for further consideration. The motion is very important and worthy of support, because even a superficial reading of the Bill shows clearly that it is deeply flawed. Whatever the worthy intention or purpose of this Bill may be, the Bill is so flawed and is so far from meeting that worthy purpose that it does not deserve second reading in its present form.
On June 23, 1983, the Minister of Employment and Immigration under the previous Liberal Government appointed Judge Rosalie Abella to head a royal commission on equity in employment. Judge Abella tabled her report last November. The principal recommendations of the report were that legislation enacting mandatory employment equity for employers under federal jurisdiction be presented to the House and adopted by Parliament; second, that provincial Governments be persuaded to adopt similar legislation in the areas of provincial jurisdiction; third, that contractual compliance be established for all federally regulated employers; and finally that an agency be established to enforce mandatory employment equity.
What does the Abella Commission mean by employment equity? As defined by Judge Abella, employment equity is the elimination of discrimination and the promotion of employment opportunities among four target groups representing 60 per cent of the population: women, native people, disabled persons and visible minorities. By the way, Judge Abella preferred the expression "employment equity" to the one that had previously been in use. "affirmative action".
The Government, under the rules of the House, is required to respond to reports like the report of the Abella Commission that are tabled in the House. The response by the Government to the Abella Commission Report gave the impression that the Government was going to respond meaningfully and to some substantial degree to the recommendations of the Abella Commission. First, the Government said it would extend employment equity to federally regulated businesses with more than 100 employees, although it would not deal with the smaller firms, even though they are large in number and may well be the place where many women and visible minorities are employed. Second, the response spoke of extending employment equity to government purchasing. It indicated that the Government would be committing its contractors to employ-
October 31, 1985

merit equity and that those not meeting the commitment, provided the contracts were for over $200,000 for goods and services, would not be given future contracts. Furthermore, the response of the Government indicated that the Canadian Human Rights Commission would be responsible for seeing that the provisions the Government would put in place in response to the Abella Report were followed.
The Government finally presented a Bill to the House on June 27. That is the Bill we have been debating for some days now and the Bill to which this motion applies. As 1 suggested when I began my remarks, the Bill has a very worthy purpose. Clause 2 of the Bill reads:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the work place so that no person will be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfilment of that goal, to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the same way but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences.
When I read that Clause at the beginning of the Bill, I said to myself that that sounded great. But then I asked myself what the Government was going to do as spelled out in the rest of the Bill to make this purpose come true in a meaningful and significant way. I read the Bill and I re-read the Bill and I read the Bill again. 1 found absolutely nothing in it to assure that the laudable purpose of the Bill as set out in Clause 2 could be put into effect.
The Bill says nothing whatsoever about contract compliance even though the Government promised in its response to the Abella Report that contract compliance would be part of its policy on employment equity. The Government, in its response, created the general impression that there would be something meaningful in its legislation to carry out what 1 think we all agree is a very worthy purpose. However, this measure contains nothing whatsoever regarding mandatory enforcement of employment equity. There is nothing about it that is compulsory. No matter how flagrantly an employer may ignore its provisions, there is no way that the Canadian Human Rights Commission or any other body can issue an order that the Bill's provisions be carried out and, that if they are not carried out pursuant to that order, that proper charges can be laid.
The Bill has no provision for a separate monitoring agency. 1 have already said that according to the initial response of the Government, the responsibility will be conferred on the Canadian Human Rights Commission. The Minister has said something about promising additional resources for the commission but there has been no indication of the additional amount of money and staff members to be provided.
The Auditor General's Report tabled just the other day made very clear that the Canadian Human Rights Commission is simply overloaded with work under its existing jurisdiction. There is no way, even with the best will in the world, that the Canadian Human Rights Commission, even with additional staff, resources and budgets, can monitor the provisions of this Bill. In any event, the monitoring would be without any meaning, purpose or effect because the Canadian Human
Employment Equity
Rights Commission wil not have any authority to enforce the provisions of this Bill over any employer who wants to ignore it even though the Bill nominally may apply to such an employer.
The Bill sets no targets or guidelines for employers to follow. The Bill contains some very vague wording. The Bill has a laudable purpose, but even for employers who have the best will in the world and want to live up to the purpose of this Bill, there is nothing for them to do by way of seeking advice or guidance on how to live up to the purpose of the Bill in a meaningful, binding and significant way. As I have already said, there will be no penalties whatsoever when, as is bound to occur, there is an unwillingness on the part of employers to conform to the Bill.
I think we have learned over the years that when it comes to setting standards of acceptable conduct on behalf of the community, these standards are not going to be followed and do not have any meaning unless there are sanctions applied to those who do not live up to them. That is a great flaw in this Bill among other flaws. In fact, the Bill does not provide for definitive standards of conduct. It simply sets out a purpose which we all consider laudable.
We in the Official Opposition have been urging the Government to implement fully and promptly the recommendations of the Abella Report concerning employment equity as they affect federal agencies and Crown corporations. We say that the Government must ensure that the legislation is mandatory, comprehensive and enforced. This is exactly what is not contained in this Bill. Therefore, no matter how laudable its purpose or intention, the Bill is fundamentally flawed and must be sent back to the drawing-board.
The motion before the House to give the Bill the six-month hoist should be adopted by the House in the interests of the important objective of employment equity. If we do not adopt this motion and the Bill goes forward, we will be perpetrating a cruel deception bound to lead to frustration and disappointment on the part of the target groups designed to be helped by the concept of employment equity. They deserve better. The country deserves better. As a result, this Bill should not be given second reading. It should be sent back to the drawing-board for a complete redrafting. Therefore, this motion should be adopted and we should get on to some other business rather than continue with this Bill.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, you will not be surprised to see me entering this debate. You and I, Mr. Speaker, belong to that very large number of Canadians who have been described, quite correctly, as ethnics. "Ethnics", in Canada has come to mean people who are neither of Anglo-Saxon nor Francophone origin.
Mr. Speaker, I know that over the years, you and I have seen in many places, until very recently, large employers who would not hire ethnics. I am speaking of some of the largest

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
retail and sales organizations in Canada. I am speaking of the banks and the trust companies which were, until not so many years ago, forbidden territory for those who were not white, Anglo-Saxon and Protestant. It took a long time for us ethnics-and I am now speaking about the older ones whose parents came before or just after World War I-to be accepted for employment in some of the largest business organizations in Canada. Similarly, accommodations in terms of housing and apartments for rent were areas in which people from certain groups, from various ethnic origins, were not acceptable. There were summer resorts where people of certain religious or racial affiliations were not acceptable. To a large extent for the older ethnics that type of discrimination has disappeared. Unfortunately, however, that discrimination which we experienced years ago is now here, prevalent and active for newer ethnics, the non-white people who have come from Asia, Africa and the West Indies. Studies have been conducted which show that their chances of gaining a job are probably one-third of what the job opportunities are for people who are part of the majority. I spoke about this matter several days ago and other Members have put a great deal of the evidence on the record.
We now know that there are other groups which are discriminated against. For example, the handicapped. I have in my hand a telex from Mr. Jim Derksen, Chairperson of the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped in Winnipeg, which states as follows:
The Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, Canada's major coalition of disabled persons, feels betrayed by the employment equity legislation being proposed by the Progressive Conservative Government. The legislation, as presented, bears no resemblance to the election promise made by the Progressive Conservative Party during the 1984 election campaign. Canadians with disabilities were promised contract compliance affirmative action along the lines proposed in recommendation 26 and 27 of the Obstacles report. This commitment has not been kept in the proposed legislation which does not include any legally binding contract language.
We received the same response from women's organizations which have also reacted sharply. They know that despite the gains which have been made by some women others are still discriminated against. Women are still second class citizens. I would like to put just a few facts about the situation pertaining to women on the record. The average earnings of a woman in the paid workforce are only 60 per cent of the average earnings of a man. Women workers are still confined to job ghettos. Some three out of five work in clerical, sales or service occupations. Some 42 per cent of families headed by women have incomes below the poverty line, while 62 per cent of single elderly women live below it.
The best way to deal with this matter is to refer Hon. Members to the reply given to me by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who when 1 challenged him to do something about the increasing number of Canadians-more than four million who, in 1984, live in poverty-said that we are going to do that by finding jobs for them. Jobs will help but not jobs at the lowest end of the scale.
In recent years we have educated and trained more women in professions than ever before. There are now more women doctors, lawyers, architects and engineers than there ever were
before. However, the number of them who are working for the Government has not increased by very much. The number has not increased because we do not have a mandatory equity program. The federal Government Departments, the people in charge of the employment offices of the Government, have not been instructed that it is a high priority for them to employ women who are qualified.
I would like to mention just one other group which is really at the bottom of the ladder in every situation, whether it be education, health, housing or employment. I speak of our native people. In cities in western Canada, in Winnipeg, Regina, Calgary and Vancouver, there is a rapidly increasing number of native people. They are moving into the cities because the economic base on most of their reserves does not permit them to earn a living which will keep them in comfort. We have schools in the core area of the city in which 95 per cent of the students are native. Their opportunities to gain employment, even if they are qualified, are very slight.
Some studies have been done with respect to this situation and we have some facts and figures with regard to it. They show very conclusively, as far as the federal Government is concerned, that the need for an affirmative action program for indigenous peoples which was first identified in 1973 has not worked. The program has not met the objectives. The problem is simple. The Departments did not follow the voluntary guidelines of 1978 because they were voluntary. They were not held accountable for the lack of progress. Since the Office of Native Employment was set up hirings have increased; but they still fall below the 4 per cent level identified by the program. Indeed, the current level of native people in the Civil Service is just over 1 per cent and hardly any have jobs which are of any importance.

This program will not work on a voluntary basis as is proposed in this Bill. This program will only work if we have mandatory programs and if those public servants, those who are involved in the hiring for the federal Government-and I say the same about the provincial Governemnts-are given targets. We are not saying to hire people just because they come from minorities. We are saying hire minority people who have the qualifications. It has not happened up to now and it will not unless we have mandatory programs.

Mr. Speaker, the decision of my Party to support the motion to hoist Bill C-62 was not done without considerable thought and deep and careful consideration. I might say that that attitude seems to be in contrast with the great regulatory with which closure is being imposed on the House these days, even on Bills which will be of enormous cost to the taxpayers. However, let us leave that for another day and another opportunity.
We have decided to support a motion to hoist this legislation because it is a small and very thin Bill, and I do not mean only in its pages, words and clauses, but a very thin Bill in substance. It is a vessel which contains next to nothing. It largely ignores the much-heralded Abella report. The Abella
October 31, 1985

royal commission and the recommendations contained therein are not reflected in this legislation.
It has been said on more than one occasion that a Bill like this cannot rely upon voluntary compliance. There has to be some mandatory program for affirmative action or employment equity. There must be some compliance provision, some mechanism to enforce the provisions of this Bill. The only way one can get into trouble with Bill C-62 is if one fails to fill out a report. What if one reports no action at all? If it is a large company doing business with a Government, perhaps the Government may take some action but then again it may not.
The Obstacles report stated that the net should be much more extensive than simply the large companies which do business with the Government, that it should include even small companies, for instance, those doing about $20,000 worth of business a year with the Government. Without trying to sound unkind or unduly critical, I have to agree with a colleague who said that Bill C-62 represents a lip-service approach to employment equity. It wants to make use of the Human Rights Commission in order to carry out what is somewhere behind the Bill, a long way behind it, and that is good intentions. The Human Rights Commission of Canada, as we all know, is a very over-taxed institution. It needs more resources and needs them now. The Minister has promised these resources some day in the future but it needs them now in order to deal with the backlog of work it faces.
All that is really required in Bill C-62 is for a company to declare that it is an equal opportunity employer. Voluntary action in a field like this, as you and I both know, Mr. Speaker, is next to useless. We need something which has the possibility of giving effect to the ideals we love to espouse in this Chamber.
Kathleen Ruff, a spokesperson for the Canadian Association for the Mentally Retarded, stated on June 12, 1985, and 1 quote:
This is not employment equity, this is misleading advertising, this is a dishonest statement on the part of the government. It is a broken promise.
Mr. Jim. Derksen, national chairman of the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, who has been quoted in this debate, said that this legislation is a betrayal of election promises.
It is interesting to contrast the Bill with the fanfare which accompanied the introduction of it. This Bill was supposed to do quite remarkable things in terms of rights for Canadians. It was to remove employment barriers, not shift them gently aside, and to promote equality, not take a small modest step in the direction of equality. The employment equity working paper went even further in telling us what this legislation was going to do, and I quote:
Employment equity constitutes a major step in the efforts to ensure that women, aboriginal peoples, visible minorities and persons with disabilities participate fully in the economic life of this nation.
What an outrageous assertion of what this legislation was to accomplish. One would think from all of the promotion that what we had here was a bold new move. I do not believe it is even one small step. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that it bothers
Employment Equity
me in no small measure to see that one of the designated target groups within this legislation are the aboriginal peoples of Canada. It is very far-fetched indeed to believe that Bill C-62 is going to provide equality of opportunity for the aboriginal peoples of Canada and will allow them to participate fully in the economic life of this nation. Judge Abella knew that and told us that quite clearly. In her report, Judge Abella demonstrated that she had grasped very quickly and very well the magnitude of the problems facing Canada's aboriginal peoples. She looked at the date-and it has been quoted in this House and in many Government reports-which clearly indicated that native people have the lowest participation rates in the labour force of any group of people in the country. They have the highest unemployment. Did Judge Abella say to us that to help the aboriginal peoples we must bring in a modest, meek, mild, little piece of legislation which says to the companies which do business with a Government: "On a voluntary basis, give them the chance for an interview"? Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? Most aboriginal peoples do not even get inside the building much less past the receptionist and into the office where the interviews are given. They never get that far. How is Bill C-62 going to help them?
Judge Abella stated on page 4 of her report, and I quote:
For native people, equality in employment means effective and relevant education and training, accommodation to cultural and geographic realities, a primary voice in the design of the education, training, and funding programs established for their benefit, meaningful support systems, and the delivery of services through native-run institutions.
That is where I would take my stand, Mr. Speaker. If this Government would bring in a separate Bill-let us call it "equity employment opportunity for aboriginal peoples in Canada" or "access to employment" based on that recommendation-there would be something to support. The Government knows this because the National Economic Conference, which was a very worth-while undertaking-I am sorry it turned out to be more fanfare than substance-and the papers which were submitted to that conference are valid. In one of the papers submitted regarding access to employment for native people, the first sentence reads: "Access to employment for native people is a complex and difficult issue to address". It goes on to say:
Severe social and economic problems are compounded by the realization that the majority of Native people have lower education levels than most Canadians, are unskilled and generally have inadequate opportunities that would allow for positive changes.
Our paper attempts to highlight these problems with a view to identifying some alternatives that, if undertaken, would increase the opportunities for more Native people to acquire higher education, adequate and relevant training, and ultimately, create the access to employment.
Although Bill C-62 claims that it will do something in this regard, it is because it does nothing that we have introduced this motion. We want the Government to take the solid and commendable motivations of the other side and put them to work in order to give us a Bill with some teeth. We want the Government to up-grade the quality of this Bill and give us a

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
separate piece of legislation to meet the very complicated needs of the aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I am proud to support Bill C-62 as it shows the tremendous progress made by the Government to ensure equity in the Canadian labour force. I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill does not deal with all the problems related to employment equity, but it is still a good starting point. This initiative will have a substantial impact on the human resources and the economy of our country. It will also be a basis for the development of our human resources, which will have surprising results within a few years. In addition, this development will take place in a context of economic renewal.
I say this because, in my opinion, the principle of employment equity makes perfect sense economically. Indeed, by implementing effective mechanisms, we shall be able to a great extent to meet our economic objectives. The competitiveness of Canada will depend on its ability to adjust to any future change. Our productivity will depend not only on technology, but also on the extent to which the employers are able to manage their human resources. Productivity will increase if the members of the designated groups can be trained and integrated into the labour force. Nowadays, the Government must put its resources to the test if it wants to stimulate the economy while bearing the social costs resulting from the problems of disadvantaged workers. By continuing to underutilize our human resources, we are jeopardizing our own future. We can no longer afford to ignore the skills available to us, to import an unprofitable labour force and to tolerate the high rollover of manpower or an inadequate matching of required qualifications and available skills. Such an attitude hinders our productivity.
Our country is facing a dilemma: Either we continue not to develop our human resources and to bear the costs of the transfer payments and social upheavals caused by our failure to face international competition, or else we take a concerted approach to ensure employment equity and harmony between the labour force and the labour market. Ensuring employment equity will cost money, Mr. Speaker. We shall need resources to make an exhaustive analysis, to amend and adjust our present employment systems or to create more equitable ones. However, if we consider that employment equity is a valid effort to improve the productivity of our labour force and to appease the general controversy, the results achieved should be positive as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, we must take steps in order that women, native people, the handicapped, and visible minorities learn the skills needed to be competitive on the market-place, if we are to make major changes over the next decade.
This is why employment planning has such an important role in the overall plan to ensure employment equity. It provides us with a perfect opportunity to devote money, time
and effort to human resources. It puts the accent on training and employment development which are closely related to the private sector.
Further, each of the six programs under it fulfills the needs of target groups.
Bill C-62, as I said, Mr. Speaker, is but a first step. This Government has not been in power for very long, but we have identified the problem and have acted accordingly.
Also time is ripe for requesting the co-operation of the industrial sector and special interest groups. We must choose between thinking that no major choice is required, and seriously considering the opportunities offered by human resource management and employment equity.
The opportunity to put our economy back on course is there. Let us make sure that the recovery benefits all Canadian men and women.
I also listened closely to the comments-if the word is right-made by the Opposition parties. What I find interesting is that they even slap themselves on the back about a report entitled Equality for All to try and put forward an interpretation that no one ever had in mind. Mr. Speaker, in case you were not aware of it, I personally was a member of that Committee. When, in her introductory paragraph to the chapter dealing with employment equity, Judge Rosalie Abella defined the phrase "employment equity", she had this to say:
Employment equity is a means of eliminating discrimination faced by many Canadians in that area. According to Judge Rosalie Abella, it is a strategy designed to do away with the present and residual effects of discriminatory actions and to establish equity in competition for employment opportunities for those men and women who have been arbitrarily excluded. It requires-
And this is very important-
-a special blend of various components, namely what is essential, what is fair and what is practical in the work place.
Mr. Speaker, we have the first recommendation in that chapter, Recommendation No. 59, which states, and I quote:
We recommend that legislative measures be implemented to establish equity employment programs at the federal level to require employers: (a) to set up and maintain employment practices aimed at abolishing discriminatory obstacles; and (b) to increase the proportion of women, natives, handicapped persons and members of visible minorities in the work place, without however imposing mandatory quotas.
This indeed is exactly what Bill C-62 is all about. We never said, when we referred to mandatory measures, how to go about making them mandatory.
Mr. Speaker, if that committee was established, the subcommittee on equality rights, it is because there was a problem. Yet, in private discussions with various people, everyone supports motherhood, everyone supports equity. But when at the collective level it comes to ensuring that such a concept will be implemented, then things are different. It is for that reason that a committee was set up, it is for that reason that the committee made its recommendations, although its membership was aware that the way to solve this long-standing

October 31, 1985

problem was not to impose penalties for non-compliance, but rather to prompt people to change their views through incitations, and that if this does fail, we could then impose penalties.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I will say this, because enough is enough. I was listening to a comment from the Opposition-I do not remember exactly who was speaking-the reference being that this was a Liberal report. This is false, Mr. Speaker. It is not a Liberal report, but a forward looking report that was supported by a majority of Conservative Members.
Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry that my time has expired, because 1 would have more to say.

Mr. Speaker, today's debate goes to the heart of the kind of society in which we, as Canadians, want to live in the future. As 1 think about that society and consider the questions we are attempting to deal with in Bill C-62, there are four occasions that stand out in my mind that I would like to share with the House of Commons.
One occasion which strikes home in a particularly strong way occurred during the election campaign last year in the debate that was organized by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. I recall watching the debate and noting the interesting exchange which raised many important questions. There was one question in particular which I believe would strike all Members of the House of Commons very hard. This very tough question on behalf of women in Canada was: "Why should we trust any of you politicians to put into effect the measures that you have talked about to us here tonight? Why should we trust you?" While that is a tough question, it is one to which we must respond not through words but through action.
As 1 think about this piece of legislation before us today I cannot help but consider that this Bill represents a failure to respond through action. It is this failure that the women of Canada were making us face in their tough questions last year.
1 also think of a visit to my office by the committee of the people representing handicapped Canadians across the country shortly after I was elected to the House of Commons. They put a strong case to me that the battle for equity in our society is not just a battle that affects women. I was told that it is a battle that is equally important to those who must live their lives in wheelchairs and must face major physical handicaps that constrain and diminish their lives. As legislators we obviously cannot entirely overcome these constraints but we can take serious steps to establish equity in the workplace for these people who are physically handicapped.
1 think of the presentation made to our action group on jobs in Toronto this past March by Carol Tator of the Urban Alliance. That group, drawing together black Torontonians in particular, talked to us about the absolutely incredible results of a study they had conducted in Toronto to test the depth of discrimination within perhaps the most liberal of our cities.
Employment Equity
They found that 28 per cent of employers felt that non-whites simply could not meet job performance criteria compared to whites. Some 82 per cent of employers had no policy to deal with discrimination in the workplace, and, in one-third of the 438 work-places tested, preference was given to white applicants over non-white applicants who were equally qualified. This revealed a systematic discrimination against visible minorities that is simply not acceptable in Canada in 1985.
I think of another occasion during that action group trip when representatives of Indian groups, native groups in northern Ontario, spoke to us about their efforts to establish training systems which would provide for their special training needs. Each of these occasions brought home to me the sense of a Canada of inequity, unfairness and inequality, which is not a part of the Canada in which 1 want my children to grow. It is not part of the Canada in which 1 want to live.
I believe we all must have a commitment to equality, not only because it will give a chance for a fair life to those who presently experience inequality but because it will give all of us in this society the experience of living in a community in which equality does exist. It will give us a sense of human solidarity in a society in which there is fairness for all. That is what equity in a society is all about.
When the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), for whom 1 have special regard, brought forward this Bill and introduced it for first reading, I applauded vigorously. I hoped that it would be a Bill that would achieve this vision of an equal place for all of us as human beings. It was a great disappointment to read the details of the Bill and see its inability to implement this vision of equity. That disappointment has been shared by all of those groups which feel this inequality the greatest in our society.
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women has condemned the Bill as not meeting the promises that had to be met. The Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women says that an enforcement mechanism is crucial. The conclusion of the Urban Alliance on Race Relations about this Bill is that the reality of the Government's response simply does not take into account the complexity, the pervasiveness and the intractable nature of discriminatory barriers. I could quote from the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped who say that this Bill leaves this group of perhaps the most disadvantaged of our countrymen feeling betrayed by this proposed employment equity legislation. That sense of betrayal is not what we should be supporting as a House.
I urge the Government to withdraw this Bill, to rethink it and to bring back a Bill that will put affirmative action into place with tough enforcement mechanisms to make it work.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate for what is the second time for me on Bill C-62. I am pleased about my second opportunity. Perhaps

October 31, 1985
Employment Equity
1 can use the seven or eight of my 10 minute allotment on a more specific focus than my first participation on this Bill.
I am pleased to support the amendment moved by my friend in the New Democratic Party that will have this Bill hoisted for six months so that the Government, and particularly the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), can have another go at the blackboard. It is important this Bill receive extra work and a finishing on two accounts. First, it is a poor Bill and a weak one. It lacks the courage I would have loved to have seen in it. Having said that, let me preface those remarks by saying I do not think there is a Member in this House, regardless of political stripe, who does not agree that the Bill is a timely one in the sense of trying to achieve equality for all and in trying to achieve for all Canadians equality in the workplace. That principle is shared by all Members. What we should be asking as parliamentarians is whether this piece of legislation will simply speak to equality or deliver equality to the Canadians mentioned in the four target groups.
It is my opinion, and one shared by a number of different organizations from the target groups right across the country that the Bill will not deliver the equality it was intended to deliver. The purpose is far nobler than the process or the mechanism incorporated within Bill C-62. The programs are not stringent. They are not mandatory. There is no specific mention of an enforcement mechanism in the Bill.
The Minister and the Government have said since its introduction that the Canadian Human Rights Commission will have the opportunity to be the watch-dog on a national basis for an employment equity program. We all know that the Canadian Human Rights Commission is very busy these days. It is a body that reacts on a one to one, case by case basis. It is also a commission, as highlighted by the Auditor General's report, that is backlogged with a huge number of complaints from Canadians whose rights have been abused.
I must ask you, Mr. Speaker, and this House whether it is fair and proper to put the watch-dog mechanism to the Canadian Human Rights Commission when it is already strapped for financial and human resources. There should have been an enforcement mechanism, provided independent of the Canadian Human Rights Commission and this Government, to ensure that the words in the Bill would be reality.
There is no mention in the Bill of contract compliance. There is no mention of the federal Department and bureaucracy where visible minorities are reflected in the bureaucracy only to the tune of 1.2 per cent. Yet we have what the Government says is a monumental Bill on employment equity and it lacks all the various sectors I have outlined.
There is no criteria for the programs to be carried out by the different entities announced in the Bill. There are no penalties going to the firms or Crown corporations that do not attain employment equity. However, there is a penalty that if you do not report, you can face a fine of up to $50,000. If we are to fine anybody, we should be fining on the basis of not achieving what this Bill wants to achieve rather than saying that if you
do not submit a monthly or a yearly report, a letter or a document, you will be fined. That is a perverse sense of logic.
On the second aspect, Mr. Speaker, we should be holding off this Bill for another six months because introduced in this House the other day we had the Equality Rights Report which speaks boldly to the rights of Canadians in the four target groups. This report accepted the visible minorities report, Equality Now and it reflects the Abella Commission. It was the Abella Commission which triggered this piece of legislation. The Abella Report said two fundamental things. First, you need a mandatory program, one that will deliver equality rather than only speak to it. The second thing Judge Abella mentioned was an enforcement agency. Both these central elements in the Judge's report which triggered this legislation are missing.
Expectations were raised upon receipt of the Abella Report that the Government would move swiftly on its recommendations. The Government did not do that. We should be reviewing and rethinking what Judge Abella said, what Equality Now recommended and more recently, what the equality rights committee said, a committee made up of Members from all sides of the House who removed the partisan element that is always alive and well in every issue. We should be paying attention to those three landmark pieces of work, and we should reflect those recommendations in Bill C-62. As a Parliament, we should be united in trying to improve this Bill.
I rise not to see the defeat of this Bill from a partisan view- that is the furthest thing from the truth-but I rise on this occasion to urge my colleagues on all sides that the Bill merits a review and a strong number of amendments to ensure that employment equity will be delivered, will be a reality and that Canadians from the four target groups receive not a special privilege or a gift but receive what is yours, mine and dutifully theirs as Canadians, namely equality for one and all.

In referring to visible minorities, I should like to indicate that 1 have the good fortune of having a large Sikh community in my constituency. Not many weekends go past when I do not spend a few moments speaking with individuals and small groups that lay out in a very precise way the discrimination which they face on a regular basis in the workplace and, actually in some cases, before the courts of the land. It is a sad situation.
Many of us hoped that Bill C-62 would go a long way toward alleviating some of these problems and removing discriminatory practices by requiring firms, which do business with the federal Government, to enact affirmative action programs that provide equal opportunity for all workers doing business with the federal Government. It is a small step in that direction in that the Bill itself, by its presence, recognizes that discrimination exists. However, the disappointing aspect is that it will only relate to those companies with more than 100 employees, bidding on contracts of $200,000 or more. In other words, it is too restricted. It is restricted to a handful of firms doing business with the federal Government. What about those firms not doing business with the federal Government? It does not require firms to introduce affirmative action programs to assist the disabled, native people, visible minority groups or women. It simply requires them to keep statistics on the numbers of women, disabled, visible minorities and natives on staff and to keep lists of the positions they hold. This will be reviewed on an annual basis. It is a very watered-down version of any kind of action which the Government may be taking to eliminate discrimination in the workplace.
However, what I find amazing is that not many days ago an article appeared in The Globe and Mail headlined "United States big business bullish on affirmative action laws". Large corporations in the United States have found that if they introduce mandatory affirmative action programs, it is actually good for business, is good for the economy and is good for their corporations. They have done well and, in the end, it has been to their advantage in a variety of ways.
We have to ask our friends in the Government to take note of the fact that the corporate sector in the United States is bullish on affirmative action programs. Hopefully it will motivate Hon. Members opposite to go into committee with an open mind, if it ever gets to committee. We felt that it was so weak and inappropriate at second reading stage that it should be hoisted for six months and hopefully come back in a form which is affirmative action, which has some teeth and requires firms doing business with the federal Government, as a starting point, to provide equal opportunity for visible minorities, women, native people and the disabled. In other words, it would really do something, as opposed to this "limp wrist, Milquetoast, Casper the Ghost approach" to affirmative action programs.
I want to indicate for the record that there is no shortage of statistics which describe the situation faced by women in the workplace of a discriminatory nature. I should like to read a few statistics which are relevant to women. The average
Copyright Act
earnings of women in the paid workforce are only 60 per cent of the average earnings of men in the workforce. Therein lies, I suppose, one of the most obvious areas of discrimination. By and large, women workers are still confined to work ghettos. Three out of five work in clerical, sales or service occupations. The best example can be found by walking into one of the banks in Ottawa. As one walks through the door, one notices that all persons doing the public relations work for the bank are low-paid women or poorly paid, one might say. If we ask bank tellers what they are paid after five years or ten years of employment, I do not think we would feel proud of the salaries which they are receiving. However, if one looks through the doorways into the back rooms, one finds that the management positions are filled by men. It is probably the best example or model of the discriminatory workplace.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is not necessarily true.

I hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). Perhaps 3 per cent of the people involved in bank management are women, but that certainly does not reflect what ought to be happening. Those major institutions ought to be providing some leadership as opposed to being perhaps one of the most outmoded, medieval types of work structures when it comes to equality.
The statistics indicate that 42 per cent of families headed by women have incomes below the poverty line and that 62 per cent of single, elderly women live below the poverty line. If we look down the list, we find that over the last 10 years the average unemployment rate for women was 9 per cent, whereas the average unemployment rate for men was just over 7 per cent.
I notice that you are signalling, Mr. Speaker. 1 hope to have an opportunity to continue when this matter comes before the House once again.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It being 5.46 o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed on today's Order Paper.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUDIO AND VIDEO RECORDINGS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUDIO AND VIDEO RECORDINGS
speechtext:
that Bill C-227, an Act to amend the Copyright Act (private recordings), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have great pleasure in moving second reading of Bill C-227, an Act to amend the Copyright Act in respect of private recordings. The purpose of the Bill is

October 31, 1985
Copyright Act
to allow the making of a recording through the use of home video recorders and tape recorders by individuals for their personal use, where such recording is made from a public broadcast, noting that any compensation under the Copyright Act has previously been made to the holder of the copyright by the public broadcasting system used for the original broadcast.
Subsection 17(2) of the present Copyright Act reads in part as follows:
The following acts do not constitute an infringement of copyright-
(c)	the making or publishing of paintings, drawings, engravings-
(d)	the publication in a collection, mainly composed of non-copyright matter,
bona fide intended for the use of schools-
This Bill would add the following section: aedlO
-the making of an audio or video recording of a work, where such recording is made by an individual from a public broadcast for his or her private use, and the recording is not used in a commercial nature, nor sold, exchanged, bartered or given as a gift.
In other words, the Bill would add to the Copyright Act something which will please thousands of people throughout the country.
In March, 1984, Statistics Canada carried out a survey of home appliances, in which survey forms were sent to 8,857,000 residents in Canada. The results of this survey showed that 1,104,000 VCRs were already in use. I might add that if members of the general public in a country respect the law, they will obey it. If the law is not respected, more and more will disobey it. Bill C-227 will correct that error.
In The Globe and Mail of July 12, 1984, a story appeared under the headline: "Copyright Jungle: Which way out?". It was written by Paul McGrath, a Toronto freelance writer and broadcaster. In the story, the following appeared:
-out of this miasma has recently come the first clear suggestion of proposed government action: From Gutenberg to Telidon, a federal White Paper on copyright. The title suggests that the Government has looked closely at the entire range of intellectual property and the document is as thorough an outline of the proprietary rights as could be expected. Based on a five-year series of background papers, the White Paper deals, most importantly, with the urgent copyright issues that have been the topic of public debate.
I would draw your attention to this sentence in particular, Mr. Speaker:
-duplication of film and video material for private use will not be an offence under the new Act-
That was from the White Paper issued in 1984 by the previous Government. Surely this makes common sense when a tape is made for a family's own personal use. The actors, performers and producers of a television broadcast have been financially compensated by the broadcasting company and therefore should not be entitled to additional funds if their broadcast is viewed at 4 p.m. or 10 p.m. rather than at 3 a.m.
It must be kept in mind that this amendment will not allow recordings to be made for rebroadcast, sale, gift or trade but for personal viewing only. This Bill makes copying legal for personal use.
Why do people make copies? First, it may be that a particular program is being shown at a time that is inconvenient for the family to watch. Rather than racing away from work 30 minutes before quitting time in order to catch a continuing soap opera or rather than staying up until 3 a.m. to see a particular program, it is far easier to record the program and view it at a time suitable to their schedule. Second, with the rapid changes in today's technology, it may be that a copy of a program was legally purchased by an individual but machinery or equipment on which to play it has become defunct or non-existent. This happened with 8-track tape players. In this case, it is necessary to duplicate the program onto a new format in order to continue enjoying same. Many citizens would carry out such a duplication but would not repurchase the same old recordings in a new format, nor should they.
In today's society, we encourage science and technology to create new devices in order to speed up the processing of information. The present Government has even appointed a Minister of State for Science and Technology. This is good. Yet existing copyright laws penalize the public for using the very devices we are encouraging our scientists and technologists to create. Video recorders and tapes have become a multimillion dollar industry employing thousands of Canadians in what is, because of an antiquated law, an illegal and improper business under existing legislation. This Bill would change that.
For any Member of Parliament who may not think that this is a serious matter or feels that it may be dealt with at a later date, may I point out that this Bill also covers an illegal activity that Members of Parliament may well be performing in their own offices right here on Parliament Hill. If a Member of Parliament makes a recording at home or in his or her office of any proceedings of the House of Commons, he or she breaks the law even when recording his or her own speech and even when he or she did not know that the broadcast of the House of Commons is covered by copyright. Ignorance of the law, they say, is no defence.
Through some special arrangements which state that the House of Commons is not subject to the Copyright Act, the OASIS Network is able to record and show Video Quorum each day so that Members of Parliament can see how statements made by the leaders of all three political Parties are carried in the press. Do that at home and you break the law. It is time the law changed to keep pace with today's society.
Up until five years ago, 8-track tapes and players were very popular. Many people purchased pre-recorded 8-track tapes. Today it is almost impossible to find 8-track tapes or players on the market. Most recording studios and stereo systems have changed to the cassette format. As a result of this, thousands of members of the public are left with hundreds of 8-track tapes. I was once in a home where there must have been 300 of them on the shelves. The entertainer or composer was paid a fee by the individual consumer at the time the 8-track tape was purchased. Whether the song or recording is now played directly by means of an 8-track player or converted to a
October 31, 1985

cassette and played by means of a cassette player will have no effect on the composer or producer provided that the converted tape is not publicly sold.
Many of today, modern hits are sold on long-play records. These are recordings on which there may be up to 12 songs or numbers on each. In most cases, the LP was purchased in order to listen to one or two songs only. For a member of the public to purchase the LP and then record one or two songs from each LP onto a cassette tape for his own personal listening should not be an offence as the performing artist was paid under the Copyright Act at the time the LP was purchased. Further, in most cases, the finished cassette tape would not be available through the market-place.
Since technology is constantly changing entertainment systems as it did when it changed from mono to stereo, 8-track to cassette and LP to the new laser discs, these changes are making existing systems for playing recordings obsolete. The composer has absolutely nothing to do with technological changeover from one type of stereo system to another. For members of the public to be able to continue to enjoy the works of art they have already purchased, they must be able to convert the recordings they own to a system that can be played on the machinery they own without fear of having broken the laws of Canada.
At the present time, there is on the market a device which allows a consumer to play cassette tapes in an 8-track player. There is not, however, any device which enables the consumer to play 8-track tapes in a cassette player. Surely no one is suggesting that a cheque should be sent to a composer when an individual consumer plays a cassette tape in an 8-track player. Why then should it be illegal to re-record an 8-track tape onto a cassette tape for playing in today's modern equipment?
In the field of video recordings, there are presently four formats on the market: VHS, Beta, disk and the new eight millimetre format. Already the disk format has lost popularity with the consumer and the Beta format may be following the same route. It is expected that within the next decade, at least two of the other formats will disappear from the market-place. There is also the possibility that all four formats will vanish from the market-place and be replaced by a new type of format not yet introduced as changes in this field are taking place almost daily.
Members of the public should not be condemned to breaking the law if they use copying devices to change movies they have legally purchased from one format to another. As I previously mentioned regarding cassette and 8-track tapes, there is presently a device on the market which allows the consumer to play a Beta tape in a VHS player. There is no logical reason why the producer of a movie should be paid an additional royalty simply because the film was viewed by playing it in a machine of a different format.
It may be argued that the Copyright Act is coming before the House of Commons at some time in the future and that all changes should be made at that time. We have been waiting for changes to the Copyright Act for many years. I suggest that even though the Act may come before us shortly, that is
Copyright Act
no reason for refusing to make the Act sensible and reasonable at the present time by passing this Bill. As a matter of fact, it could well be that the discussion in committee of this particular Bill would be assurance that when the total Copyright Act comes before the House, we would be better prepared to handle it in a sensible and logical way.
In closing, I again emphasize that the making of audio or visual recordings of broadcasts for the personal use of the individual family must not be used in any way in a commercial nature or sold, exchanged, bartered or given as a gift. I have never made any such recordings but some one million people in Canada have. I suggest that the House would be wise to give reason to their voices by sending this Bill to committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUDIO AND VIDEO RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill which is before us this evening. Bill C-227, is effectively a Bill to make an exemption from the Copyright Act for home copying purposes. The fact of the matter is that there is a great deal of home copying in Canada. Canadians are pirates, outlaws and criminals in terms of stealing intellectual property from creators. Most Canadians are copyright pirates in some way or another, be it the Sunday school teacher who xeroxes her lessons for her Sunday school class or an ordinary Canadian who tapes programs from the CBC on a home video cassette recorder. Common as this is I suggest it does not make it a good enough reason to change the law in the direction proposed by the Hon. Member. Just because a great many Canadians are breaking the law does not mean that we do not need that law at all. That law is there for a purpose.
We know that artists receive a bad deal from our country. They serve the country well. They subsidize the creative lives of Canadians to an enormous extent, far more than they should. Burdens are being placed on them to give of their services voluntarily; and when they are not recompensed by royalties for their work it means they have to suffer unduly. It seems extremely unfair. They have to pay the same for their groceries, their rent and mortgages, and they have a tougher time doing it. In fact, a much higher proportion of our artists live in poverty than people in other occupations.
Copyright does entail intellectual property. This property is created by people using their minds or their hands. It can be stolen just as other types of property can be stolen. I suggest that the consequences of this type of theft are not altogether harmless, even though the crime may take place in the home and it may be something which has the most innocent of purposes. Indeed, the type of uses which the Hon. Member has pointed out are quite proper and reasonable forms of use for entertainment. There is no suggestion that there should be an exemption which would allow anyone to take commercial advantage of this form of copying. However, even this use in the home has consequences for the owners of copyright material.
I had the pleasure of sitting on the Copyright Committee for the better part of last year. In the committee artists told us

October 31, 1985
Copyright Act
that they did not want to see any exemptions in the Copyright Act which would impair their very precarious livelihoods. They did not want to see any further exemptions. Indeed, they asked us to close the loopholes where exemptions already exist.
The whole thrust of the Bill which is before us is to take us in the opposite direction from-
