speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in fact, the extent of violation of copyright is enormous. This is a question in which technology has created problems which we never imagined it would. More than one million households in Canada now have copying equipment, VCRs, of some sort or another. It is expected that that number will increase greatly every year and that very soon half of the households of Canada will have some type of recording equipment. This means that there will be an enormous use of this type of equipment. We do not know to what extent it is being used to copy material for which other copyright royalties might have been paid. However, we do know that a great deal of it is. It is estimated that as high as 90 to 95 per cent of the machines are used to some extent for copying copyrighted materials. They are not just being used to delay, to take out commercials or to switch times in order for a family to watch a program later in the day than its airing time. A lot of this use is to replace what might otherwise have been purchased. People go out and buy a record, a video cassette, or whatever, and when that happens the artist concerned receives a royalty. However, if there is another recording made then the artist does not receive that royalty.
The effect of this new technology can be seen in a Quebec study which shows that revenues from video rentals are now greater than revenues from movie attendance. So people who are showing movies are getting away from paying royalties and, as a consequence, artists are suffering.
There is clearly no way to control home copying and there is no suggestion that we should try to think of any way to control it. I suggest that the right proposal is to not forget about the problem and say: "Go ahead and do it," but to institute a practice such as the one proposed in the copyright report. That is a matter I deal with in my own minority report because I think I have a slightly better way of dealing with it. In either case, the idea is to allow for a levy on the tapes, on the cassettes and the equipment itself. The moneys thus collected-and there is some dispute as to how it should be collected-would be in lieu of royalties. This would mean that artists would receive some compensation to make up for the loss of royalties they do not receive as a result of home copying. Perhaps this compensation would only be a small part of the royalties which artists might have received if they had sold
their works directly and if there had not been any home copying. However, it is at least a recognition that they have a right to be paid for their work and that they need money to pay for their groceries the same as everyone else needs money. It is at least a partial recognition of this fact and it seems to me to be a reasonable one.
Artists have been asking for this type of provision and, indeed, it became clear in testimony to the subcommittee that a great many Canadians are concerned about the difficult lives artists lead and that they are ready to see that there is more compensation paid to them. Even though people recognize that they would have to pay more money there was a great deal of acceptance of this principle. It was felt that it is time we stopped making artists pay all the subsidies for our culture. It is time for the burden to be more equitably borne by Canadians in order to get artists out of poverty and in order to give them more recognition for the work which they do.
I think there is a great deal of public support for measures such as the ones proposed in the copyright report. That is to say, in lieu of royalties being paid for home copying there should be a levy on all of the equipment for making the recordings and all of the mechanisms needed for doing it, be they tapes, cassettes or whatever new technology brings us. It has been recognized that this money should somehow go to the artists.
The way I propose it be done is by way of a tax because that is money which can be directed. We received a recommendation from the National Film Board to the effect that the money should go into Telefilm Canada and be directed toward further production works. That is certainly a good recommendation. The majority report for the committee on copyright recommended a straight royalty. My concern in that respect is that there would be a large outflow of funds from Canada as a result because so much of the copying which is being done is copying of material of a foreign origin. That would mean another burden being placed on the arts community with respect to money leaving the country. In a period in which we have had substantial cut-backs, it did not seem to me to be the best procedure to follow. Nevertheless, it is a clear recognition that artists deserve to be paid for the work which they do. I support that move as such, although I would prefer to see a different method put in place.
The idea of providing compensation by way of levy has been accepted in a number of other countries. We are not the only country considering this move. Nor are we the only country where artists have been demanding that such a move be implemented. We are not the only country where the public has reached the state in which they consider it an acceptable and fair provision.
Legislation to compensate copyright owners for home copying has been enacted, or is in the process of being enacted, in Austria, West Germany, Hungary, Norway, Sweden, the Congo, Finland, Iceland, Turkey and France. That is a sizeable number of countries. Further, legislation is under consideration in Denmark, Italy, the Netherlands, Switzerland, the United States and the United Kingdom. In Canada itself
October 31, 1985

we have the beginning of a recognition. It has not worked out well, I might add, but nevertheless, there is the beginning of a recognition in Quebec with a tax of $2 on blank tapes.
The delivery of this money into the arts community has been fouled up rather seriously and we very much regret that. Nevertheless, it is a recognition and the principle is the right one. Clearly, the mechanism to get the money delivered to the artists should be put in place immediately.
As to the amounts, there is debate as to what would be a reasonable compensation to the artists concerned. In the United Kingdom, the recommendation is up to 10 per cent for audio tapes; and 5 per cent for video tapes. In France it is 56 cents per playing hour. In Finland it is up to 60 cents. West Germany it is down to 7 cents. This is just to give an idea of the amount of money which consumers might expect to have to pay in addition in order to see that artists are compensated.
With respect to machinery, in the case of Iceland, it is 4 per cent. The United States is considering levies in the order of 10 per cent to 25 per cent. In Canada, the recommendation is that the tariffs would be established by the Copyright Board.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would simply point out that we do have other options. This ongoing problem of artists not being compensated-and with home copying going on in great numbers-can be dealt with in a reasonable way. We are Canadians. We are masters at practical compromise. We should not just ignore the problem and put in an exemption in the Copyright Act, but we should make the exemption contingent on there being another and fair method of compensation for our artists. They have been serving us very well and I ask that we in this House give them the support they deserve. They have been paying the way for Canadian culture all too long. Let us share the burden with them and see that their needs are really justly met.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUDIO AND VIDEO RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have to ask that Hansard be amended to excise that word. I am not sure that it is parliamentary.
The distinguished Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has introduced a Bill in this House to amend the Copyright Act and it is a great privilege for me to speak to his Bill. I have followed the career of this distinguished parliamentarian for many of the 45 years he has served the public and I admire his initiatives and vigour very much.

Bill C-227 aims at allowing private recordings of a public broadcast for personal use.
I would like to thank the Hon. Member for having supported the motion. This issue is very important and complex.
Copyright Act

At first, the provisions of this Bill appear straightforward. However, the Bill provides an excellent example of a problem of immense proportions which affects the life of every Canadian. The problem concerns the law of copyright. At the consumer level it is copyright law which sets the rules under which market forces determine what music is heard, what records are made, what film are seen, what books are published, and what programs are seen on television.
The problem can best be described in terms of two ends of a spectrum. At one end there is the creative talent of this country such as authors, poets, composers, film producers, script-writers and publishers. In order to earn a living, creative interests depend upon copyright royalties being paid for the use of their creations. At the other end of the spectrum there is the user of these creations, the general public, who pay royalties by buying books, sound recordings, and theatre tickets but who also want to be able to copy these works with a variety of recording devices.
There is a dual purpose in the copyright system. On one hand, copyright stimulates creativity by granting exclusive rights to creators. On the other hand copyright responds to the public interest in the widest possible availability and dissemination of the subject matter of copyright. New copyright legislation is required to restore the balance between the legitimate interests of creators to be paid for the use of their works and the needs of users to have access to those works.
Before individual recording devices were available, creators were able to control, and be paid, for the use of their creations. For example, a broadcasting station would pay for the right to broadcast a program and the owner of the program would license the broadcast. Modern reproduction technology, which is used in individual homes, cannot be licensed in the same way. Now creators do not have control over their works and, in the case of home taping, are not being paid for their use.
The solution proposed in Bill C-227, although direct and relatively simple, does not address the need of copyright owners to be compensated for the copying of their works. The owner of the copyright in a film or television program has the right to authorize the broadcast and the right to authorize the reproduction or copying of the film or program. When a broadcaster pays a royalty to broadcast, the payment is for broadcast only. The royalty does not cover what would be paid to copy the film or program. Copying is a separate use from broadcasting which requires a separate payment.
Bill C-227 proposes that no compensation should be made for copying at home. That is one solution. However, it is not the only one. Another solution would be to pay compensation to copyright owners on the basis of a levy or tax on blank tape or recording equipment. As my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) said, this solution to the home taping problem is used in a great number of countries and others are contemplating doing so. Right here in Canada, the Province of Quebec introduced, in 1983, a tax of $2 on each blank tape sold to compensate for royalties lost due to home copying. My information is that, unfortunately for

October 31, 1985
Copyright Act
creators in the Province of Quebec, that money finds its way into general revenue and not into the hands of the creators.
When the magnitude of the problem is assessed the solution proposed in Bill C-227 may not be the most appropriate. It is estimated that 1.8 million Canadian homes have a video cassette recorder. Home taping is no longer an isolated activity. As home taping grows in magnitude so too does the damage to creators. In a larger context home taping is just one particular example of revising the copyright law to balance the needs of creators and the public.
New reproduction technologies are one of the reasons why the Government is committed to a complete revision of the law. The law in question is the Copyright Act which was first enacted in 1924. This law is hopelessly inadequate to deal with new technologies such as home taping, computers, satellites and photocopying machines.
Because of the inadequacy the Government has already taken steps to completely revise the law to bring it up to needs of the present day. In January of this year the Minister of Communications referred all matters of copyright revision to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Communications and Culture for a complete and thorough review. Its subcommittee has considered over 300 briefs and submissions from interested parties and has heard 111 witnesses at public hearings. The subcommittee filed its report to this House on October 10. It contained recommendations for appropriate solutions to the problem addressed in Bill C-227 as well as to the many other problems involved in copyright revision. The report recommends that a compensation system be introduced together with an exception from copyright liability which would permit home copying. The system which has been proposed will be considered by the Government. When a copyright Bill is introduced in the House full debate on the most appropriate solution to home copying will take place in the context of the overall revision of the copyright law.
To prejudge this involved an complex work by proceeding to deal with one of many related problems in isolation would be ill-advised. First, it would be a duplication of effort to have two separate parliamentary debates to consider the same problem. Second, the complexity of revision of the copyright law requires a concentrated and intense intellectual effort. All of the many issues are interrelated. The selection of a particular solution to one problem will dictate the choice of similar solutions to other similar problems. Without a consistent approach the revision of the law will be a hodge-podge of unrelated solutions with no central policy to further the cultural goals of the Government, or the country.
The issue of home taping addressed in Bill C-227 illustrates the complexity of copyright revision and the consequential need for the already completed committee work on revision. The Bill proposes one particular solution to the home taping problem. The committee has proposed another. An examination of the issue reveals not only the complexity of the problem but also alternative solutions to it. I have already stated that modern technological development has called into question the ability of existing copyright legislation to adequately protect
the interests of copyright owners. This had led to appeals for revision of the Copyright Act to incorporate the same form of compensation for copyright owners for use being made of their works. In contrast, Bill C-227 proposes that no compensation be paid.
The present copyright law provides copyright owners with the exclusive right to reproduce a work. There are some exceptions to this exclusive right, the purpose of which is to strike a balance between the needs of creators and the needs of users. There is no specific limitation in the existing copyright law relating to the copying of copyright works for personal use. It is not certain whether some limited personal use might be permitted as falling within the exemption for fair dealing set out in the Copyright Act. In any event, it has been generally concluded that the concept of fair dealing is no longer able to deal with the new reproduction technologies such as home video recorders and photocopying machines which involve, in the aggregate, multiple reproduction of entire works. Consequently, it is generally concluded that the issue of copying for personal use should be dealt with in its own right.
Two polarized solutions are possible. One is to exclude home taping from the category of infringing actions by means of a specific exemption. The other is to construct a system which would provide for reproduction with compensation paid to copyright owners by either the manufacturers of the reproduction equipment or those who purchase blank tape.
The amount of home taping is increasing. Statistics tell us that the number of people purchasing video recorders has increased enormously over the past few years. Opponents of a compensation scheme for home taping argue that the amount of home taping cannot be quantified. It is true that the extent to which copyright owners have been harmed by home taping is disputed. But, however large or small the harm, it is clear that home taping is a major use of copyright works for which creators receive no payment.
The inability of copyright owners to control or to receive fair compensation for copying may disrupt the economic foundation of the motion picture and television production industries. Copyright owners face an even greater risk of economic loss than they did before in a competitive market-place. Their works are subject to widespread, uncompensated copying. Many directors, writers, actors, cinematographers, craftsmen and others depend for their livelihood on revenues earned by copyright works. They are harmed, as are many others, as a result of home taping. The loss is also occurring in many segments of the market-place: displaced attendance at movie theatres, prerecorded cassette sales lost to home-made copies, displaced viewing of cable and television transmissions and reduced royalties from broadcasters due to the adverse effects of time shifting. This amounts to direct economic harm to Canadian creators and copyright owners.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-227 would deprive copyright owners of any compensation for home taping. From what I have just outlined, it is apparent that the enactment of
October 31, 1985

legislation, which would deny copyright compensation for home taping, requires a thorough and careful examination. The issue is complex and its solution is far from clear. A parliamentary reference of this problem, as well as the whole matter of copyright revision, to the subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture has recommended that compensation should be paid. When the copyright revision Bill is tabled in the House a full debate on the very complex problem of home taping will take place. Mr. Speaker, any further debate should be postponed until the complete copyright revision Bill is introduced.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUDIO AND VIDEO RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-227 proposed by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), I would like to bring to the attention of the House certain broad public policy considerations and some particular aspects of the Bill which must be taken into account. I would like to thank my distinguished colleague, the Member for Bow River, for flagging the attention of the Department of Communications and the House of Commons to his particular concerns which I know are shared by many Canadians. The Member for Bow River has done the House a considerable service in bringing to our attention an issue which is of significant interest to consumers, creators, the film and sound recording industries, and those charged with developing a national copyright policy and legislation.
The Hon. Member for Bow River will know that in Canada today national copyright legislation is ridiculously outdated and is unresponsive to the needs of creators, entrepreneurs and users of copyright material. While the Copyright Act of 1924 was perfectly suited to such mechanical devices as player piano rolls and wet photography, it is totally inadequate for today's electronic communications age. Technological developments and advances are not addressed in the present law, nor is any provision made to accommodate change. I refer to television, cable systems, photocopiers, computers, satellites and video machines by way of example.
When we speak of the need to revise the legislation dealing with copyright, and indeed the Government has announced its intention to do so at the earliest possible opportunity, we must not forget the principle upon which the present law is founded. The present Act grants to creators exclusive private property rights in their works. These rights provide the legal foundations for industries which rely on the property rights of creators. Copyright legislation enables creators to exploit their works through the publishing, film production, sound recording and broadcasting industries. In turn, it is copyright which provides the legal basis for the creation and operation of these industries.
By licensing their rights to these industries creators make it possible for consumers to read books, see films, listen to music and enjoy television. Consumers and users have a wide choice of cultural material available to them through the operations of the market-place. However, because of the technological change the present law has become more and more unsatisfactory to creators, the industries using copyright material and,
Copyright Act
indeed, to consumers. This is because the law is uncertain and those who wish to benefit from the law or to use copyright works are uncertain as to their rights and obligations, particularly in the context of using the new devices made possible by technical advances.
Since 1977 the Departments of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Communications have been engaged in studying and reporting on the necessity and urgency of revising copyright legislation. In May of 1984 the former Government tabled in the House of Commons a White Paper on copyright revision entitled From Gutenberg to Telidon. That paper discussed revisions and advanced certain proposals based on the considerations of protecting creativity and responding to technological change. A major shortcoming of the copyright White Paper, Mr. Speaker, was its failure to identify the significant relationship that copyright legislation has to economic growth.
That deficiency was rectified on November 8, 1984 when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in delivering his address on the economy in the House, tabled the document A New Direction for Canada-An Agenda for Economic Renewal. In that document the Minister of Finance identified and underscored the particular and strong importance that copyright legislation has for economic growth, particularly with respect to the creation, transmission and processing of information. The Minister said:
Canada's Copyright Act, unchanged since 1921, has been overtaken by new technologies. This has created abiguities and uncertainties and has, in some cases, left Canadian copyright owners with less protection or compensation than would be available to them in other countries which have more modern copyright laws. Impacts are particularly significant for the vitality of our cultural and computer services industries. This is a real obstacle to economic growth, particularly in an economy which is increasingly service-oriented, with a growing role for the creation, transmission and processing of information, and in which automation may be a powerful source of productivity gains.
A broad-based update of Canadian copyright legislaton is needed to create an appropriate and balanced copyright environment. Much preparatory work has already been done and extensive consultation will continue.
It is manifest that it is a central policy concern of the present Government to address and resolve the issues created by technological developments. These developments represent major challenges to the interest of creators and the industries based on copyright.
Technological advances have made it possible to use copyright materials in ways not envisaged in 1924. Copyright works which are broadcast can be picked up and delivered around the world by satellites, and photocopying machines can reproduce books at the touch of a button.
It is because of these changes and the legal uncertainty of the present law that revision of the legislation is urgent. I recall that the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) moved a motion in the House on January 24 that all matters of copyright revision, including the White Paper on Copyright be referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture for examination and report. The motion received

October 31, 1985
Copyright Act
unanimous consent, thus approving the urgent need to get on with the revision.
1 lay stress on what I consider to be a key phrase contained in the November 8, 1984 statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) almost a year ago on the need for copyright revision. Ele said:
Much preparatory work has already been done and extensive consultation will continue.
Given the necessity of taking into account a range of factors and considerations in revision of copyright legislation, I believe fully consultation is fundamental to arrive at a consensus which will permit an equitable revision of the law. The committee report represents another stage of consultation which will receive a full debate when a copyright Bill is tabled in the House as soon as possible.
In considering particular proposals to revise the law to permit certain things to be done, it is my view that the broadest possible approach should be adopted. That approach should include taking into account not only the views of those affected by any change in the law, but the results which would flow from adopting any change. Here, in dealing with the possibility of making recordings or of certain works, the interests involved appear to be those of the creators of the work being broadcast, the owners of the copyright in the work being broadcast, the broadcasters themselves, and the individuals who make the recordings.
This activity, popularly called "home-taping", is an issue of some importance as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has pointed out. The omnipresent video-tape recorder has made possible the recording of broadcast material an everyday occurrence.
The issue has been litigated in other jurisdictions with varying results. Indeed, the Committee on Copyright Revision of which I had the honour to be a member, had representations made to it that the incidence of home taping is seriously affecting the interests of copyright owners. By attempting to make copying a non-infringing activity, are we saying, in effect, that technology which makes copying possible should prevail over the rights of those who create works of the mind? Is such an exception compatible with Canada's international responsibilities? Is it in the public interest to provide such an exception? If the exception is enacted, what principle can be derived in order that it may be applied in other instances where similar or even different exceptions are sought?
These are very important questions which are at the heart of the many issues that will be debated when the copyright Bill is introduced in the House. It is my view that this particular matter before us cannot be addressed and answered in the narrow confines of a Bill designed to address a particular issue. Rather, I think that the answer has to be sought in the broadest context of the committee's report and the soon to be introduced copyright Bill where the many and manifold aspects of this question can be fully addressed.
I sympathize with the Hon. Member for Bow River and the sentiments behind this particular Bill. As I said earlier, I know
that he shares the concerns of many Canadians about what is to happen regarding this particularly important aspect of home taping, which is among the some 137 recommendations we made in the Subcommittee on the Revision of Copyright. We received more than 300 applications and heard from 111 different witnesses. Many of them were speaking on the same topic that the Hon. Member for Bow River has raised this afternoon. Hundreds of thousands, indeed millions of words were submitted to the five members of the subcommittee, three of whom have spoken in this debate this afternoon. It was an enormous job in the course of 10 months, even through the summer, to come up with recommendations which we believed would update the copyright legislation from the archaic law that has existed since 1924 up to the 1980s to the end of this century, until some other parliamentary subcommittee will have to meet in the year 2035 or 2050 A.D. to deal with the technological developments that will have taken place.
As the Minister of Finance and I have pointed out and as the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) and the Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) have made clear, it is not possible to consider one aspect of copyright revision in isolation. It must be put into the context of those 137 recommendations made by our subcommittee. We must ensure that whatever is enacted in the form of legislation is consistent with the economic statements that have been made by the Government.
If the Hon. Member for Bow River and his friends have any concerns that the home-taping regulations are not fairly dealt with in those recommendations of the subcommittee he will know that once the legislation comes before the House of Commons it will go through the normal legislative process and back to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
I say for the benefit of any hon. Member who is concerned about any of the recommendations which are made by the Government of Canada in that legislation, it is in that legislation where amendments can be brought forward. That is when we can debate all of the matters we have been discussing in the last 10 months. That is how we can bring about true copyright revision for the people of Canada, legislation which we believe to be a charter of rights for creators.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUDIO AND VIDEO RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of legalization of home taping of audio and video material is one which certainly warrants discussion. However, with utmost respect for my hon. colleague, the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), it would be premature to adopt the solutions proposed in Bill C-227.
In January of this year the issue of copyright reform was referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture which, in turn, formed the Subcommittee on the Revision of Copyright to examine all aspects of copyright revision, including the issue of home taping. In referring to that subcommittee, I cannot help but congratulate the participants who spent many long hours this past summer hearing many presentations. That subcommittee advertised for submissions and held public hearings in June. A number of submis-
October 31, 1985

sions addressed the issue of home taping and the subcommittee issued its report on October 10. The report contained 137 recommendations dealing with virtually all aspects of copyright law reform. Recommendations 93 to 96, both inclusive, addressed the issue of home taping or home copying in particular. The report dealt with all forms of home copying, not just recording from public broadcast.
The subcommittee recommended that audio and video home taping be permitted, subject to a royalty on the blank tapes and the recording equipment. This royalty would be paid to domestic and foreign copyright owners on the basis of tariffs approved by the Copyright Appeal Board. It did not recommend compensation for broadcasters. The minority opinion, while it agreed that copyright owners should in some way be compensated for home taping, felt that the compensation should be on the basis of a tax on blank tapes and equipment as opposed to a royalty. It favoured the tax approach because it was concerned with the outflow of royalties, while a tax would allow revenues to be channelled to creators and copyright owners in Canada.
Under Item 70(16) of the Standing Orders, the subcommittee requested the Government to respond to its report. It would be premature to act on this very complex issue until we have had the benefit of the Government's response.
The following are some of the points which must be considered in developing a policy on home taping. I will expand on some of them in a few moments. Audio home taping from broadcasts is a fact of life, Mr. Speaker. Many Canadian households have an audio cassette recorder that can make reasonable, and even high fidelity recordings, from FM broadcasts which can be used in personal stereos, cars, boats and at home. Such devices have been available for many years.
Video home taping is also commonplace. Somewhere between 10 per cent and 30 per cent of Canadian households now have a VCR, depending on what figures you use. Many studies have confirmed that these machines are mostly used for time shifting or library purposes. In either case, copyright owners are not pleased with the result.
How does one balance the realities of newly available technology in private households and traditional compensation to copyright owners? This is a delicate balance and any discussion must take both factors into account.
Because of this balance, one must examine carefully changing the law in the way the Hon. Member for Bow River suggests. The problem is that copyright owners and broadcasters would demand some sort of compensation for any such change in the law. Many experts will support them. To accomplish this, as we will see, is extremely complex and may or may not even be desirable.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, and in view of the Government's commitment reiterated here this evening to an overall revision of the law, I recommend that we wait until the Government has responded to the report of the subcommittee before acting.
Copyright Act
I would like to expand on a couple of these points. Home taping is a fact of life. It takes place in several ways; for example, video taping for time shifting purposes. A recent study in the United States showed that, as the largest single use of VCR was the recording of afternoon soap operas so that they could be viewed in the evening. Of course, many people time shift other types of programs as well. Perhaps someone somewhere might even time shift proceedings such as these.
Second, we have library or collection purposes. Many viewers tape TV broadcasts for repeated viewing or permanent storage. This type of taping typically involves movies or collectable dramas or comedies, such as Star Trek or M.A.S.H. Radio broadcasts are also taped, not so much for time shifting as for more or less permanent collection purposes. Many young people tape FM broadcasts of new hit records and thereby avoid, so the argument goes, having to buy the record. In fact, for less than $300 one can now buy a portable mini studio that will play and record FM and cassettes in stereo and even duplicate the cassettes for a friend, and I might add, with surprisingly good quality.
Some would say that this proliferation of emerging technology may actually be beneficial to copyright owners. This theory works in the following way. By creating new uses for recordings, technology has encouraged consumers to buy them. Indeed, this makes some sense. A consumer can purchase a record and make a copy of it to use in the car or personal stereo. If, on the other hand, a person makes copies directly from the radio, at some point the user has to hear the inevitable commercial message, which is how everyone in the system gets paid. Although there are studies that indicate that this is the case, most copyright owners, broadcasters and advertisers loudly disagree.
I wish now to summarize possible problems with Bill C-227 and then explain some of the points in greater detail.
The solution may be too simple. It fails to reflect that certain home taping off the air is seen by some as an illegal act, while on the other hand some types of home taping off the air may actually benefit copyright owners.
Second, the Bill is based upon the premise, as stated in the explanatory note that:
-compensation under the Copyright Act has previously been made to the holder of the Copyright by the Public Broadcasting System used for the original broadcast.
Most copyright owners, broadcasters and advertisers would strenuously disagree with that assumption.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-RESIGNATION OF WOMAN MANAGER. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INQUIRY
PUBLIC SERVICE-RESIGNATION OF WOMAN MANAGER. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the case of Isobel Goligher is representative of those of a large number of Canadian women. When an injustice is done to any person it is wrong and it should be resisted. I would be speaking today as if Isobel Goligher were the only person to be affected by the kind of discrimination she has experienced. But, she stands for many women, which is one of the reasons she is continuing her fight.
Let me explain the facts. Ms. Goligher was made chief of the EDP Section of Supply and Services in the London district office on September 22, 1980. This was the first time a woman had achieved a post this high in that Department. Within a year, on August 25, 1981, she resigned from that position under duress. What happened in that time?
Ms. Goligher was very competent; she proved her competence. The information we have from her evaluation, for example, indicates that she was evaluated at her probation period, six months afterward, and that Ms. Goligher's progress to date in adapting to her computer operation had been excellent. "She exhibits sound administrative qualities and I consider her a pleasure to work with". She passed her probation exceeding the Department's expectations. Yet one would wonder how a person doing this good a job could, six months later, be out of that same job.
One of the reasons her reports were so good was that she had a non-adversarial management style. This is something which makes the case a woman's case. Isobel Goligher did not have the same kind of confrontational tactics which apparently had been rife in that Department. Productivity went up and complaints went down. Morale was much better and staff worked harder as a result and felt happy about their jobs.
We might think the Government would be pleased with these developments. These are the kinds of managerial skills we want to encourage. Indeed, it is one of the hopes of the women's movement that as women move into management positions the beneficial aspects of a different kind of socialization and a more co-operative spirit, could be achieved.
Let me note, and let me be very clear, that productivity did go up. It is curious that she should be told later that she was not managerial material, evidently because she was not adversaria! enough. She was too chummy with members of the union, for example, a statement made about her. What a curious thing to say when the evidence is so strong that all the results of this chumminess were better morale and a better job done for the people of Canada.
Ms. Goligher was told when she was promoted that her case would be a test and that people would be looking at her. What the Department failed to do, I regret to say, is look at the managers around her to be sure that she got the back-up she needed.
We do not need to have women tested when they are promoted to managerial positions. It should not be surprising that a women can handle such a position. This is not the first time a woman has been in a managerial position. That should not have been a matter for the test. We do know that in some work environments they are not ready for women yet.
Perhaps there should have been more back-up to ensure that she was accepted and that she would be able to continue in the job. That is why this is an important case for us today. If we are to have employment equity, if women are indeed to be promoted, they must get that back-up. It is not good enough to have a program on paper which indicates that women will be promoted in the Public Service; it is extremely important that there be adequate back-up and that their competence and participation are treated on a reasonable basis. If there are problems, they should be looked into promptly and solved, so that ill will does not develop.
What can be done about it? The only remedy available at this point is to have an independent inquiry established by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Ms. Goligher has exhausted all means at her disposal. She has tried a grievance and the Public Service Commission. No other remedies are available to her. This is why she and the Public Service Alliance of Canada have asked for an independent inquiry.
There has been much correspondence, including correspondence with the present Prime Minister and when he was Leader of the Opposition. He took some interest in the case and hoped that it would be resolved. I would suggest that it is not good enough to take an interest or to say, as he said: "Over 30 months have passed since Mrs. Goligher's resignation and, as public interest in this case appears to be increasing over time, 1 hope that you"-and this was directed to the Minister in question-"will personally give this case the consideration it merits".
I will tell the House what consideration this case merits. It merits an independent inquiry and action accordingly. There should be a possibility of this inquiry establishing, as I expect it would, that Ms. Goligher is perfectly competent and should be in that position. The relevant authorities should be given the option of putting her back into that position, or another suitable position should be found for her.
October 31, 1985

It is important that justice be done. It is important for us in Canada, now that we are beginning to see women treated equally in the workplace and beginning to get promotions, that women be able to do their jobs. This is why I call upon the Government this evening to set up an independent inquiry to make employment equity a reality, not make it mere rhetoric.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-RESIGNATION OF WOMAN MANAGER. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member bringing this matter forward. I want her to know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) are concerned about it, and I want to put some facts on the record.
The Hon. Member made the point that the Prime Minister has taken an interest in the matter. I think it is important for that to be on the record. The Prime Minister and the Government are adamant about equality for women in the Public Service.
My information is that Mrs. Goligher joined the Public Service in July, 1976. In September, 1980, she was promoted to the position of Chief of Eletronic Processing Section in the London regional office of the Department of Supply and Services. Obviously that was a responsible supervisory position. My information is that she was a competent employee and that management, at no time, had any intention of dismissing her for any reason.
On August 10, 1981, she submitted her resignation without reasons, and this took effect on August 24, 1981. Since that time she has made considerable efforts to convince Members of Parliament, union officials, departmental management and independent tribunals that her resignation was submitted under duress, at a time of emotional stress, that it should be rescinded and that she should be reinstated to her position.
Ms. Goligher has made the following formal applications to independent bodies, in each case alleging that her resignation was submitted under duress and should be rescinded. The formal bodies are the following: the Public Service Commission Investigations Directorate, the Public Service Staff Relations Board, the Federal Court of Appeal, the Federal Court Trial Division and the Public Service Commission Anti-Discrimination Directorate. In every case the independent body dismissed her complaint, finding no evidence of duress or disciplinary motive on the part of management.
The Hon. Member, who in my experience does not bring forward these matters, lightly, has asked for an independent inquiry. I submit that these inquiries are about as independent as one can get. If there is some reason that they are not independent, I would like to know. In fact, I think every Member of the House would like to know. Mr. Speaker, do I have 10 minutes?

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SASKATCHEWAN FARMERS' LOSSES. (B) REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE PAYMENTS
AGRICULTURE-SASKATCHEWAN FARMERS' LOSSES. (B) REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 16 I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) inquiring as to when the Government would come forward with financial assistance for the people in Saskatchewan and Alberta who suffered as a result of the worst drought in the history of western Canada, certainly since 1937. I had an opportunity to visit Assiniboia this summer and to see some of the devastation which was clearly biblical in proportions.
On September 10, I put a question to the Minister. It was the first day Parliament came back after the summer recess. He said at that time that he was waiting for the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) to make a report and that he would have it in a couple of weeks. I put another question to him some two weeks ago, and he said that he would be taking it to Cabinet.
The real problem with the Minister is that he has no clout. I do not doubt for a moment that he wants to do something, but he has zero impact on his cabinet colleagues and on the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), because he never gets an answer to anything. I could run through a list of at least a half dozen items. Canadian farmers are waiting for stabilization payments and stabilization agreements. They are waiting for action on the part of the Government, whether it be on potatoes, sugar-beets or the farm debt crisis. The new Government of Ontario which was elected in July brought down its Budget this past week and announced a $50 million program to assist with the farm debt crisis.
It is not only that the Minister cannot get decisions; when he makes up his mind to do something he proceeds to change it. This summer he announced that he would bring in legislation fearlessly dealing with a pre-foreclosure arbitration procedure for farmers facing foreclosures or bankruptcies. He backed down on that this week right here on the floor of the House of Commons.
The disaster faced in western Canada and in terms of the agricultural portfolios of the Government are not only apparent to Hon. Members on this side of the House. I should like to refer to a Canadian Press report out of Saskatoon earlier this week which indicated:
A conference involving a who's who of Saskatchewan agriculture evolved into an Ottawa-bashing session Monday.

October 31, 1985
Adjournment Debate
I point out that this conference was sponsored by Grant Devine, the Tory Premier of Saskatchewan. It continued:
About 450 producers, grain and chemical company officials, farm leaders and a smattering of provincial politicians attended the Toward a National Agriculture Policy Conference.
Just to show that the agricultural community is totally fed up with the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), 1 will read into the record what Lome Hehn, President of the United Grain Growers, a farmer-owned grain company, had to say, according to a Canadian Press telex:
Federal Agriculture Minister John Wise and Charles Mayer, Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, are not the men who can make fundamental changes in Canadian agriculture policy, Hehn said:
"Our lobby should be with (Prime Minister) Mulroney and (Deputy Prime Minister) Nielsen, not with Mr. Mayer and Mr. Wise," Hehn said.
Hehn went on to say that that is why it is so fitting that we have this conference with Premier Devine. Obviously the problem is a massive one. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will deliver to the Minister that message from the farmers of western Canada who are totally fed up with the inaction and lack of decision by the Government.
Clearly there is a massive agricultural disaster in western Canada costing somewhere in the order of $2 billion. The Saskatchewan western wheat pools have called on the Government for an assistance program of $50 per seeded acre in order to help get the producers through this disastrous situation. It is time the Government stopped hobbling around on this matter and made it clear to the agricultural producers on the Prairies and in the drought regions that it will come forward and provide this assistance which is simply desperately needed in western Canada today.
There is no excuse for putting this matter off any longer. The report the Hon. Member for Assiniboia was working on last summer was brought before the Government a month and a half ago. It went to the Cabinet a couple of weeks ago. It is time the Government made a decision and announced the assistance it will make available to the literally thousands of farmers, many of whom are already in a difficult financial position. It is time the Government got those cheques in the mail.

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING (A) CONSTRUCTION OF FRIGATES IN MONTREAL. (B) THE SITUATION IN EAST MONTREAL-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
SHIPBUILDING (A) CONSTRUCTION OF FRIGATES IN MONTREAL. (B) THE SITUATION IN EAST MONTREAL-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who spoke before me took a stand, but it was down on his knees. That is normal for him.
October 31, 1985

1 think that everyone is aware of the problem which now exists in Montreal East. Because of the inertia of this Conservative Government, Montreal East could lose 5,000 jobs. At this very moment, they are 5,000 workers who are unable to decide whether they can buy Christmas presents for their children.
1 know that the Parliamentary Secretary will read me a text prepared by officials and tell me that so many thousands of jobs have been created.
Mr. Speaker, my question was addressed mainly to the Minister of Supply and Services and concerned the risk of a close-down by the Vickers plant in Montreal. The problem is that, in a spirit of equity and to distribute jobs equitably in Quebec and the rest of Canada, the previous Government has decided to grant contracts for the manufacture of three frigates to the Versatile Vickers shipyards in Montreal to ensure employment equity with the Lauzon shipyards in Levis, and as they were not on the list of accepted bidders for the building of the frigates, the previous Government had decided to grant them a contract to repair five ships under the TRUMP Program. This was a political decision, a contract without a call for tenders, for the purpose of distributing jobs throughout Quebec and Canada and in the Maritime provinces.
Mr. Speaker, in the meantime, Versatile Vickers decided to purchase the Lauzon shipyards and to cancel the previous contract and have the frigates built in Lauzon rather than in Montreal.
The Parliamentary Secretary will say that there is nothing legally binding in the contract. This was a political decision to create jobs in the three Quebec shipyards.
Mr. Speaker, if the Government had wanted these frigates to be built in Quebec, it would not have asked Paramax to set up shop in Montreal, but in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, let us say that this Conservative Government is so very much afraid of employers, so very much dependent on their party contributions, that it will not have the guts to compel the Vickers management to live up to its previous commitments. Supposing that it cannot do that, it can say: OK. The Vickers firm has decided to build the frigates in Lauzon. The $650 million contract which the previous Government had adjudicated to the Lauzon shipbuilding yards to repair the five ships, together with the other $500 million, you are going to execute in Montreal, where it is not going to cost taxpayers a cent, the contract is not yet signed, and we are going to save directly 650 jobs at the Vickers shipbuilding plant.
Mr. Speaker, let us say that they lack the courage to talk to the company management-perhaps they are too deeply involved with the election funds-they can adjudicate the contract to Versatile Vickers in Montreal for the next ships which would require repair jobs, and the Minister had forbiden all shipbuilding firms to bid, supposedly because of the ice on
Adjournment Debate
the river .. . And we know there were underhand dealings for the benefit of. .. because the decision was made after the new Minister was appointed.
Mr. Speaker, it is a human problem and a human tragedy. It is not a matter of statistics or unemployment, not a matter of principle. It is a human problem.
My colleague from Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) was with me when we met the employees of Vickers. All those people are between 50 and 55 years of age, Mr. Speaker. They all learned their trades on the job and not at school. They worked strenuously to obtain what they have today, to raise their children and look after their family.
They are proud. And I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if this Government does not move in to save the jobs of those people, their life will be shattered. They want to work, they do not want to be on welfare or live on unemployment insurance benefits. They do not want, as was announced yesterday, to pay $500 per day to have an expert look into the problem. There is no need for research, for any scientist or economist. There is only one organization in Canada which can let contracts for boat repairs and it is the Government of Canada.
The Prime Minister of Canada during the election campaign in Montreal promised publicly before a large crowd that Montreal would become an international city. Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister actually closed down Schefferville, but I can tell him that the people in Eastern Montreal will not let him shut their place down.
